col8_Comment: The council's city-wide electric vehicle charging strategy will support the rollout of this charging infrastructure enabling the uptake of electric vehicles. The core principles underpinning the development and delivery of the city-wide charging strategy are to provide a network that: Follows the best practice approach for choice of technology. Aligns with consumer preferences and current deployment trends. Aligns with wider aims within the council, including reducing reliance on private cars and encouraging modal shift (changes in travel away from private cars and towards public transport, walking and cycling). Is accessible and equitable for all. The Council will take a leading role in developing Birmingham's EV charging infrastructure, alongside our appointed EV Charge Point Network Development Partner and associated stakeholders. Council-led deployment will play a larger role in the early stages of deployment to stimulate the market and enable the required step change towards EV uptake. Public sites, such as public car parks, green parks and Council-owned land, will continue to be developed for EV deployment, since they enable the Council to ensure that: standards for full public accessibility are met, priority user groups are catered for and that there is a comprehensive spread of charge points across the city, including in hard to-reach areas.. Whilst the overall number of charge points required for the city will depend on the scale of the change in people's travel behaviours and the modal shift achieved, the EV Strategy modelled the need for at least 40% modal shift in Birmingham by 2032 as an interim step towards achieving the central government's 2050 net zero targets.

col8_Comment: Birmingham Transport Plan - We cannot tackle the climate emergency without fundamental changes to the way people and goods move around our city. The transport plan is now in the delivery phase. The Delivery Plan sets ambitious targets for delivery of transport improvements against the key principles of the Birmingham Transport Plan. It outlines how the BTP will be delivered, quantifies the scale of the challenge, outlines the spatial framework underpinning delivery, and provides a prioritised package of transport related interventions. The Delivery Plan marks a move away from mode-based planning, towards a spatial framework with four key typologies, 'Figure 13. Birmingham Delivery Plan Key Typologies', and rather than producing a list of schemes and projects, will produce packages of demand management policies and transport interventions to transform different areas of the city to improve travel. Targets from the City's EV Charging Strategy for electric vehicle infrastructure are also included in the Delivery Plan, noting that EV rollout must be carefully planned to avoid simply replacing the city's current car fleet with low emission vehicles, which will do little to reduce congestion, and fail to influence the necessary changes required in travel mode and behaviour. Informed by the Delivery Plan, the Transportation and Highways programme dictates ongoing delivery of projects to promote sustainable modes of travel. During 24/25 progress has been made at a number of sites across the city, including: Dudley Road; Midland Metro Eastside Extension; Digbeth High Street public realm; City Centre public realm; and, the Coventry Road cycle route.

Improving air quality is a corporate priority for the Council. Poor air quality is the biggest environmental risk to the public's health, disproportionately impacting the most vulnerable in our society including children, making it an issue of social justice and health inequality. We recognise air pollution as a key public health issue. We are taking a multi-agency, cross-cutting approach that recognises the policy benefits of improving air quality to be gained by other teams such as Net Zero, Planning, Future Parks, Housing, Public Health, Healthy Schools and Environmental Protection. Air pollution and climate change are intrinsically linked, sharing the combustion of fossil fuels as a common factor, with existing air pollution being worsened by climate change and many of the air pollutants that harm our health also harming our climate. col8_Comment: Published in 2022, the Essex Green Infrastructure Standards outline nine principles and standards for the protection, enhancement, creation, and management of Green Infrastructure (GI) in Essex. The application of these principles and standards through development management and planning policy will ensure the delivery of multifunctional, accessible high-quality GI. The Essex GI Standards are based on several key policy documents including HM Government's 25 Year Environment Plan; the Environment Act (2021); and the National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF). In addition, best practice case studies and illustrative examples are also outlined. There is no end year for the Essex Green Infrastructure Standards. In July 2024 ECC, in collaboration with Northumbria University, organised workshops for the Local Planning Authorities in Essex. These workshops examined the opportunities and challenges from Local Plan development from regulation 18 to 19 Plans, through to implementation (including Development Management challenges to the delivery of the policies) and potential trade-offs from delivery of multifunctional GI through collaborative problem solving and shared learning. The workshops were an opportunity to co-design new Practical GI Planning Guidance that gives practical support to mainstreaming GI into Local Plans to delivering exemplar developments for Essex in line with the Essex GI Standards (2022) and the National GI Framework at these interactive workshops.\n

ECC is investing £9.8m of BSIP funding in a range of projects including DigiGo its demand responsive minibus service and a range of projects aimed at securing growth in market town services. DigiGo will run until at least 2026, and has been expanded to cover more of Essex (https://www.essex.gov.uk/news/2023/digigo-service-extended-march-2026) (https://www.essex.gov.uk/news/2024/digigo-service-expands).

col8_Comment: Over a third of the Essex treescape is comprised of trees that are outside woodlands in rural Essex and trees planted along streets. col8_Comment: With one of the UK's longest coastlines and lowest levels of rainfall, Essex is at significant risk from the climate crisis. New Orleans is home to public parks that are some of the oldest and most celebrated in the country. For many New Orleanians, the city's iconic parks and waterfronts make them healthier and happier and provide the backdrop against which they live, work, and play.
However, the life-changing benefits of parks, recreation, and greenspace are not equitably distributed or experienced by all. Following decades of uneven investment, and with no coordinated process to prioritize 
citywide park improvements, the park and recreation disparities in New Orleans are stark: 
» Park condition assessments and walkshed analyses show that city residents who are Black, low-income, or living in a household with disability are significantly more likely to live close to a public greenspace that is low-quality or downright unsafe. 
» And park visitor mobility data indicates that in a majority-Black city, only 26% of citywide park visitors from 2019 to 2022 were Black.
For the first time in New Orleans history, the Big Green Easy offers an equitable, community-driven framework for citywide park and recreation investments now and into the future, with project prioritization that is directly informed by community needs and feedback. 

Implementation of this plan could not be more urgent. Climate change is making New Orleans hotter and more flood-prone, and community leaders are seeking new and diverse tools to address community health disparities, gun violence, and declining public trust. Strategic investments in parks and recreation can make cities more 
livable and drastically improve the daily lives and long-term wellbeing of residents. This plan offers a path forward, toward a park system that celebrates the distinct cultures and identities of New Orleans while making the city and its neighborhoods cooler, greener, healthier, 
more resilient, and more just for all.

In ensuring our developments align with our net zero 2030 action plan there are several policies in the local plan which support environmentally sustainable buildings:

Newcastle's Core Strategy
•Policy CS1 (Spatial Strategy for Sustainable Growth) requires all development to be designed to reduce carbon emissions and adapted to the effects of climate change.
•Policy CS16 (Climate Change) requires development to be sustainable, able to function effectively in a changing climate and address the impacts of climate change emissions. There are six criteria that all new residential, non-residential and mixed-use developments must meet to conform with Policy CS16 (Climate Change) of the Core Strategy and Urban Core Plan (CSUCP):
1.A good standard of building fabric, passive design and landscape measures to minimise energy demand
2.Flexible design to allow for adaptation to alternative uses.
3.A good level of sustainability through the applicant demonstrating best practice project and site management, site water use, site transport, waste reuse and recycling, the sustainable use of materials and construction techniques. 
4.Minimise a developments contribution to, and provide resilience from, the on-going and predicted impacts of climate change.
5.A reduction in whole-life CO2 equivalent emissions impact
6.Optimise the use of local renewable or low carbon energy in accordance with a hierarchy, prioritising decentralised energy schemes, followed by other renewable energy solutions and finally other lower carbon energy solutions. Where no decentralised energy scheme exists, strategic and other large-scale developments must evaluate the feasibility of providing a decentralised energy system and, where feasible implement such schemes.
Development and allocation plan: 

•SO11 focuses on reducing CO2 emission from development and future growth while adapting to the issues, mitigating adverse impacts and taking advantage of the opportunities presented by climate change. 
•Policy DM20 - Design states that development will be required to deliver high quality and sustainable design by building in 12 key aspects including incorporating measures to address the impacts of climate change and adverse microclimatic conditions.

col8_Comment:
Blue Green Newcastle (BGN) aims to better protect the whole city centre from multiple sources of flood risk.

The city is important to everyone who uses it, so the sustainable drainage (SuDS) solutions we hope to use will not only better protect the city from flooding but enhance placemaking in the local area too, by improving biodiversity, ecology and amenity. 

By using innovative sustainable drainage techniques, the project will help deliver the Council's wider visions on climate change, carbon reduction and making the city a more accessible and greener place to live, work and visit. 

The Blue Green Vision is to...
“Create environmental and social opportunities throughout the heart of our city using innovative flood and water management techniques that make us more resilient to climate change.”

Why is the Blue Green Newcastle project needed?
In summer 2012 flooding events impacted the City in a way that has not been seen in our lifetime. The heavier rainfall we experienced is a direct result of climate change, and such events will get more frequent, likely to cause more disruption and damage in the future.

Urban area, like the city centre is more vulnerable to surface water, due to the amount hard standing area. The topography of the city increases the risk too.

Several historical watercourses were covered over as the city grew and water is now managed though engineered highway drainage and sewer networks. These do not have capacity to cope with extreme rainfall events caused by climate change. 

We will also consider the impact rising sea levels will have on the City, which affects the peak height of the tidal River Tyne. This will continue to impact historic buildings and infrastructure on The Quayside, as experienced in December 2013 and 2023.

col8_Comment: The Sea2City Design ChallengeVancouver's CFRA (Costal Flooding Risk Assessment) highlighted the need to plan for future sea level rise and improve resilience to current and future coastal flooding in flood-vulnerable shoreline neighbourhoods, communities, and businesses. The CFRA identified approximately 13 sq. km of land and buildings valued at CAD $7B (2013 land value assessment) are vulnerable to flooding in Vancouver and estimated that $1B of flood management infrastructure would be needed in Vancouver by 2100.Currently underway, the Sea2City Design Challenge (Sea2City) will help inform a framework and vision to guide urban development and ecological revitalization in the False Creek floodplain, a highly valued and constrained urban waterway in the heart of the city. The design challenge has engaged two multidisciplinary teams to work co-operatively with the City and project partners to: Explore coastal adaptation approaches that respond to the social equity, economic, and ecological challenges posed by sea level rise and coastal flooding; Investigate coastal adaptation approaches for sea level rise beyond one metre; Expand the City's toolbox of coastal flood management approaches; Increase public awareness of climate change and sea level rise.\nThe City will further refine Sea2City outcomes, working with project partners, Indigenous governments, stakeholders, the public, and coastal regulators. The outcomes will inform the next phase of the City's overarching Coastal Adaptation Plan. Conceptual designs, created as part of Sea2City, will not be built immediately, but will inform next steps (including more detailed design development and planning). The City will start to take those next steps after the completion of Sea2City and will likely continue for several years recognizing the additional research, planning, technical design, and engagement that will be required to move coastal adaption forward in a constrained urban waterway like False Creek.

col8_Comment: Nature in the City completes the City of Melbourne's portfolio of strategies that are directly focused on achieving ecological outcomes. Along with the Urban Forest Strategy and Open Space Strategy, as well as numerous other plans and initiatives, Nature in the City provides an integrated and comprehensive suite of actions to achieve thriving biodiversity, healthy ecosystems, and a society connected to nature. In late 2016, the City of Melbourne released Future Melbourne 2026, a plan that details the community's aspirations for the city synthesised into nine key goals. Informed by contributions from thousands of people, Future Melbourne 2026 has 'A city that cares for its environment' as Goal 1, elevated from Goal 5 in 2008. The community has reaffirmed the importance of ecological sustainability by having the statement 'maintain the urban biosphere' as its first priority which is directly aligned with the underlying objectives of Nature in the City. The strategy also aligns with numerous international conventions and initiatives, such as the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity, the Sustainable Development Goals, the Singapore Index, and the Cities and Biodiversity Outlook, whilst placing Melbourne at the forefront of urban conservation globally. By considering our city as a wider ecosystem, there is the opportunity to actively foster connections amongst people, plants, animals and the landscape. This will create the legacy of a resilient, balanced, and healthy natural environment with a community that is connected to nature and place, is active in protecting and enhancing biodiversity, and enjoys the associated benefits to health and wellbeing. Biodiversity is intrinsically important in its own right. As well as underpinning critical ecosystem services such as climate regulation and the provision of clean air and clean water, biodiversity is at the heart of many cultural values. It is widely accepted that connection to nature and place is vital to community health and wellbeing. Traditional Owners attach great cultural significance to the species and landscapes that feature in their creation stories. This strategy recognises there are important and inevitable interactions that occur between people and nature in Melbourne, and that there is a notable opportunity to deliver positive outcomes for both when considered together.

col8_Comment: Water is fundamental to the liveability of the city and the health and wellbeing of our community. As our climate changes, intense rainfall, flooding, extreme heat events and drought are becoming more common in Melbourne and across the world. Our municipality is also experiencing stronger population growth than previously forecast. New development is increasing, with a significant proportion of this growth in low-lying urban renewal zones that are subject to flooding.To enable this growth and manage the added challenge of climate change, we need an integrated holistic approach that will provide multiple benefits. We need open space, smart flood mitigation solutions and fit-for-purpose water, recognising the role of water and green infrastructure in responding to the effects of climate change.The City of Melbourne practices Integrated Water Management, defined as the coordinated management of all components of the water cycle including water consumption, rainwater, stormwater, wastewater and groundwater, to secure a range of benefits for the wider catchment.We have been at the forefront of Integrated Water Management for many years, under the direction of our Total Watermark strategy. The first Total Watermark strategy was adopted in 2004 and subsequently revised in 2009 and 2014. Our current vision of 'a healthy city in a healthy catchment' has been in place since 2009 and is supported by a series of objectives, short and medium term targets and a four-year implementation plan. With the implementation plan coming to an end, we need to consider how the many changes since 2014 will influence our work in Integrated Water Management into the future.Focus areas This Municipal Integrated Water Management Plan (Plan) sets the strategic direction on water management across the municipality, using a place-based and catchment approach. It guides our effort, thinking and investment for the next four years.Place-based actions have been developed for Fishermans Bend, Arden-Macaulay and Moonee Ponds Creek, Southbank and the Yarra River. Implementation of our existing Integrated Water Cycle Management Plan for the Elizabeth Street Catchment has also been included in this Plan, as well as actions that cover the whole municipality and a range of place-based actions for the rest of the municipality

col8_Comment:
The Johannesburg Spatial Development Framework (SDF) 2040 - 2024 Update sets the City's long-term vision for a spatially just, sustainable, and resilient urban form. Mandated under SPLUMA and integrated with the IDP, the SDF is reviewed every five years to align with new data, policies, and development realities. The 2024 update builds on the 2016 SDF by sharpening its transformation agenda, embedding inclusionary housing regulations, and introducing the Capital Expenditure Framework (CEF) to align infrastructure investment with strategic priorities.
Johannesburg continues to face deep structural challenges. Spatial inequality persists, with many residents housed in peripheral townships far from jobs, reinforcing a costly job-housing mismatch. Urban sprawl and fragmentation drive up infrastructure costs, while low-density gated suburbs and car-oriented malls entrench exclusion. Environmental stress threatens biodiversity and ecosystem services, while large underutilised assets such as the mining belt and Modderfontein remain untapped opportunities. Post-apartheid housing delivery has often worsened these patterns, placing new settlements far from economic centres.
The framework's vision is a Compact Polycentric City: a strong inner core linked to well-connected, dense, mixed-use nodes through efficient public transport. Scenario testing showed this model outperforms sprawl and linear corridor growth, delivering better social, economic, and environmental outcomes. Five guiding themes anchor the vision: a compact city (dense, diverse, efficient), an inclusive city (equitable access to services and housing), a connected city (public transit and ICT integration), a resilient city (biodiversity protection and climate adaptation), and a generative city (strategic investment that yields long-term returns).
Implementation focuses on transformation zones: the revitalised Inner City, TOD corridors such as Soweto-Sandton, the diversification of Soweto into a true urban district, the Randburg-OR Tambo Corridor linking Johannesburg's north to Ekurhuleni, and redevelopment of the Mining Belt to integrate north and south. Supporting policy tools include mandatory inclusionary housing (30% of units in developments of 20+), density regulations, form-based codes to create walkable mixed-use neighbourhoods, in-situ upgrading of informal settlements, and green building standards.

col8_Comment: Johannesburg's bus system, made up of Metrobus and Rea Vaya, is heavily reliant on ageing diesel fleets that are costly to operate and environmentally unsustainable. Metrobus has 414 buses, but only 257 are active, many older than 17-23 years, while most of Rea Vaya's 146 buses have clocked more than 400,000 kilometres. Both systems consume high levels of diesel—Metrobus averaging 47 litres per 100 km and Rea Vaya 51 litres per 100 km—driving monthly fuel costs above R14 million and contributing significantly to emissions. The city's depots currently lack electric vehicle charging facilities, though there is strong potential to integrate solar PV systems. National and city policies, including the Green Transport Strategy and Joburg's climate frameworks, support the shift to alternative energy buses, and other cities such as Cape Town, Tshwane, and eThekwini have already piloted electric fleets, showing both the opportunities and challenges of such a transition. Financially, the current operating model is unsustainable, but a phased move to electric buses could lower long-term costs while aligning with climate commitments. The report recommends prioritising the replacement of the oldest buses, upgrading depots with charging infrastructure, securing blended financing, and investing in workforce training. Ensuring that this transition is affordable and inclusive will be essential for Johannesburg's public transport system to become more efficient, reliable, and sustainable.

The TPH Wildfire Smoke Response Strategy is TPH's protocol for responding to deteriorations in air quality due to wildfire smoke. Updated for 2025, this strategy incorporates lessons learned from 2023 and 2024, provincial guidance (opens in new window) , and expertise from TPH's internal Air Quality Response Committee. This committee was established following the Toronto Board of Health's directive to annually review and update the strategy as needed.

Environmental health, including exposure to air pollution, is one of the nine key indicators identified in TPH's 2023 Population Health Profile PDF. Climate change is recognized as a significant risk to environmental health, with increasing trends of extreme heat, prolonged heat waves, more frequent extreme weather events, and more wildfires impacting Toronto and Ontario. On a global scale, wildfires pose a growing concern, with smoke affecting air quality, ecosystems, communities, and public health well beyond the fire's immediate vicinity.

Responding to Wildfire Smoke:

- Responses are activated when a Special Air Quality Statement (SAQS) or Air Quality Warning (AQW) is issued when wildfire smoke is impacting air quality in Toronto.
- Guidance to the public at each level is derived from the AQHI Health Messages developed by Environment & Climate Change Canada (ECCC).
- Monitoring Activities: TPH activities align with peak wildfire season, as defined by ECCC, from May through September.

Latest report available at: https://www.toronto.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/8e68-CoT-CE-Ph.-2-Report-FINAL-AODA.pdf

col5_Boundary of plan relative to jurisd: Same - covers entire jurisdiction and nothing else
col8_Comment:
As part of the Long Term Waste Management Strategy, the City of Toronto is working towards an aspirational goal of zero waste and a circular economy. To drive innovation and the growth of a circular economy in Toronto, the City established a Circular Economy and Innovation unit within the Solid Waste Management Services Division, making it one of the first municipalities in North America to form a dedicated circular economy team.

A circular economy aims to reduce waste and maximize resources by moving away from the linear take-make-and-dispose approach to an innovative system that focuses on product longevity, renewability, reuse and repair. Circular economy strategies consider resource consumption and material efficiency for their potential impacts on climate change, environmental degradation, and social outcomes. Cities are well-positioned to play a critical role in achieving climate neutrality and moving to more sustainable consumption models. 

To advance more circular and sustainable consumption and achieve its waste reduction goals, the City of Toronto is developing a Circular Economy Road Map that will help guide Toronto to becoming the first municipality in the province with a circular economy. Work on the Road Map began in 2020 with the launch of the Baselining for a Circular Toronto Study. The project involved a city-wide landscape analysis, examining the economic, environmental, social and policy conditions related to a circular economy; three sector-specific material flow analyses, examining resource use and disposal in waste, construction, and the food system; and a 'business as usual' analysis of the resource consumption and waste generation by these sectors in 2030, if left unchanged. This study also identified visions and goals for the City of Toronto's circular economy transition, which will form the launching point for the development of the Circular Economy Road Map.

Once finalized, Toronto's Circular Economy Road Map will inform policy and program changes to advance the City's aspirational circular economy goals.

The Cycling Network Plan (CNP) serves as a comprehensive roadmap and work plan, outlining the City's planned investments in the near-term and intentions for the long-term. The CNP is grounded in many city policies and strategies including the Official Plan, the Road to Health, Vision Zero Road Safety Plan, TransformTO Climate Action Strategy, Complete Streets, and key recommendations in the Toronto Office of Recovery and Rebuild's Impacts and Opportunities report.

The CNP is an evolution of the Ten Year Cycling Network Plan, approved in principle in June 2016 and a culmination of significant research, analysis, and extensive public consultation. In 2019 and 2021, the Cycling Network Plan was updated to continue to build on the work of the Ten Year Plan, including updated data sources; a revised approach to short-term programming and long-term planning that better reflects the nature of capital coordination, development planning, and challenging feasibility assessments; a strengthened focus on safety and equity; and an enhanced prioritization framework.

The CNP's project mandate is to:
• Connect the gaps in Toronto's existing cycling network
• Grow the cycling network into new parts of the city
• Renew the existing cycling network routes to improve their quality

The CNP has three main components: the Long-Term Cycling Network Vision, Major City-Wide Cycling Routes, and a three year rolling Near-Term Implementation Program.

col8_Comment:
Toronto's Wet Weather Flow Master Plan (WWFMP) is a long-term plan to protect our environment and water quality in the Lake, rivers, streams and other water bodies from the rain and melted snow (stormwater).

Key objectives of the WWFMP include improving water quality along the waterfront, beaches and watercourses, protection of vulnerable City sewer and water infrastructure from erosion and reducing the risk of flooding to private and City properties during extreme wet weather. The WWFMP also provides guidance on municipal operations, environmental monitoring and public education initiatives related to stormwater 
management.

Significant progress has been made on critical WWFMP initiatives, most notably, construction of the Don River and Central Waterfront Project which is the largest and most significant stormwater management program in the city's history, the Basement Flooding Protection Program (BFPP), the rehabilitation of City stormwater management facilities, and in implementation of works within the watercourse and shoreline management programs. Policy updates to guide stormwater management for development and redevelopment have also been initiated.

Challenges due to construction cost escalation, constrained engineering and technical resources and competing commitments have impacted the implementation of the WWFMP, however key initiatives such as the construction of the Don River and Central Waterfront Project (and related projects - the Integrated Pumping Station and the High Rate Treatment Facility at the Ashbridges Bay Treatment Plant), critical end-of pipe projects and BFPP projects remain top priorities. 

Implementation of the WWFMP is funded by investments set out in Toronto Water's annual capital budget and is primarily funded by the water rate with supplementary contributions from Development Charges, and federal funding through the Disaster Mitigation Adaptation Fund.

col5_Boundary of plan relative to jurisd: Same - covers entire jurisdiction and nothing else
col8_Comment:
La Política Pública de Movilidad Cero y de Bajas Emisiones es la hoja de ruta a corto, medio y largo plazo para promover y consolidar el uso de tecnologías de cero y bajas emisiones en todos los segmentos del transporte por carretera en la ciudad, así como para fomentar prácticas de conducción sostenible. Su objetivo general es 'Consolidar la movilidad cero y de bajas emisiones como una alternativa sostenible, accesible, competitiva y atractiva en Bogotá y la Región Metropolitana'.

La formulación de la Política Pública de Movilidad Cero y de Bajos Emisiones abordó un proceso de consulta y co-creación con diferentes actores públicos y privados, lo que permitió identificar diversos factores estratégicos para intervenir y lograr una penetración efectiva de estas tecnologías. De esta manera, se definieron los siguientes objetivos específicos:
- Promover la transición de los modos de transporte motorizados por carretera hacia tecnologías de cero y bajas emisiones.
- Fortalecer los procesos de gestión, innovación, desarrollo e investigación en la cadena de valor de las tecnologías para la movilidad motorizada de cero y bajas emisiones.
- Desarrollar un entorno de comunicación, pedagogía y participación en torno a la movilidad de cero y bajas emisiones.
- Consolidar una red de infraestructura de carga inteligente, accesible y competitiva en coordinación con el sector privado.

Bajo esta estructura de objetivos específicos, se definió un plan de acción compuesto por 13 resultados y 42 productos que conducirán gradualmente al cumplimiento de los objetivos y metas establecidos. Con la implementación de la Política, se esperan lograr los siguientes objetivos:

- Para 2039, el 100% de los buses del SITP serán de cero emisiones.
- Para 2035, el 100% de los taxis serán de cero emisiones.
- Para 2028, el 100% de los automóviles y furgonetas oficiales del Distrito (propios o contratados) serán de cero emisiones.
- Para 2032, el 100% de las matriculaciones de automóviles privados serán de tecnología de cero y bajas emisiones. Para 2040, el 100% de las matriculaciones serán de cero emisiones.
- Para 2032, el 100% de las matriculaciones de motocicletas serán de cero emisiones.
- Para 2035, el 100% de la flota de T. Cargo será de cero y bajas emisiones.
- Para 2032, el 100% de los triciclos y trimóviles registrados serán de cero emisiones.

Urbana (CBI); o Índice de Qualidade da Água (IQA); os Bioindicadores (invertebrados
bentônicos); e as novas ações para biodiversidade da prefeitura de Curitiba: Rede de

Este documento é a sequência do trabalho iniciado no Primeiro Plano Municipal de Segurança Alimentar e Nutricional (I PLAMSAN) de Curitiba, com vigência de janeiro de 2016 a dezembro de 2019.
Com a produção deste segundo plano pretende-se manter e melhorar a Segurança Alimentar e Nutricional da cidade, impactando positivamente na qualidade de vida da população. Para que o II Plano Municipal de Segurança Alimentar e Nutricional atinja patamares mais elevados na busca da SAN e do DHAA no município, é necessário que sejam apontados alguns desafios para sua execução.
Esses desafios referem-se a uma dimensão mais estratégica do Plano, expressando de forma direta, quais as linhas de ação que precisam ser enfrentadas no campo da SAN.
DESAFIO 1: Criar um conjunto de indicadores de segurança alimentar e nutricional para fornecer ao município dados consistentes quanto ao impacto das ações contidas nos projetos e ou programas estratégicos do II PLAMSAN. A criação deste conjunto de indicadores é fundamental pois é reconhecida a limitada ou inexistente avaliação da intervenção pública em SAN no país.
DESAFIO 2: Alinhar os projetos e ou programas do II Plano para que possam contribuir para a realização dos Objetivos de Desenvolvimento Sustentável (ODS) que engloba 4 dimensões: social, econômica, ambiental e institucional e colaboram para produzir informações de forma organizada, sistematizada e auxiliam nas definições sobre políticas públicas.
DESAFIO 3: Fomentar o trabalho em rede efetivo entre as pastas que compõem a CAISAN a partir de um sistema integrado para o
compartilhamento de dados e informações pertinentes à área de SAN para suporte estratégico aos programas e projetos.

Istanbul Bicycle Master Plan: Istanbul Bicycle Master Plan has been prepared in order to have better experience for the unique natural, cultural and historical beauties of Istanbul, which is located at the junction of the European and Asian continents, and to increase accessibility throughout Istanbul.

Rapid urbanization, increasing population and growing area of the city have caused transportation problems for the city. Especially the traffic problems and environmental problems caused by the intensive use of automobiles make it inevitable to develop public transportation and intermediate transportation modes integrated with public transportation. In terms of sustainable urban transportation, the adoption and use of bicycles as a means of transportation has a great importance. For Istanbul, which has more than 30 million daily journeys, popularizing the use of bicycles stands out as an alternative solution at this point. In this direction, Istanbul Bicycle Master Plan was prepared in 2019 by the Transportation Planning Directorate of the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality.

In Istanbul Bicycle Master Plan;

•Creating Social Awareness,
•Increasing the Share of Cycling Journeys in the Daily Total Journey,
•Contributing to the Improvement of Social and Individual Health,
•Improvement of Existing Bicycle Roads in accordance with the Standards and Dissemination of Urban Bicycle Routes with New Projects to be Prepared
•Ensuring Active Use of 1050 km Bicycle Roads in Istanbul,
•Reducing CO2 Emissions and Noise Pollution,

Since 1999, the Spatial Planning Model (MRO) has been the central control instrument for spatial development in Heidelberg. The core statements of the 1999 MRO have established themselves as a reliable basis for political decisions and urban land-use planning. In doing so, we address key questions:
How do we want to live, work and conduct research in Heidelberg in the future?
What spaces do we need to shape a sustainable future?
How can we deal with limited space and increasing competition for space?
How can we protect and develop our open spaces for the benefit of the environment and climate?

The MRO acts as a spatial compass for current and foreseeable future developments, tasks and challenges. It specifies the goals from the STEK and examines their spatial location in the urban space of Heidelberg.
Together, the MRO and STEK form the basis for forward-looking and sustainable urban development, strengthen municipal cooperation and promote political dialogue.

En febrero de 2023, se aprobó la Ley de Economía Circular de la Ciudad de México, con el objetivo de plantear de manera integral, la transición hacia un modelo económico circular y sustentable, al ir más allá de la gestión de residuos y establecer las bases para la construcción de alternativas económicas a través de aspectos como:

- el impulso de nuevos modelos de negocio basados en el encadenamiento productivo, es decir, la coordinación entre empresas y negocios para aprovechar al máximo los bienes y materiales, tales como la minería urbana; y el fomento a negocios basados en la venta de servicios y no sólo de productos, tales como la renta de autos, equipamiento de oficinas, entre muchos otros.

-la creación de un instrumento de evaluación para que las empresas porten el distintivo de Circularidad

- la creación de un sistema público de información de economía circular para brindar información a toda la población y facilitar mecanismos de intercambio en distintos sectores para maximizar el uso de los recursos o la definición de principios y directrices dirigidos a lograr la co-responsabilidad de los distintos sectores y la población.

Es importante mencionar que la Ciudad de México es la primer entidad en federativa en lograr la aprobación de una ley de economía circular con un enfoque integral como el que prevé la circularidad.

col8_Comment: La Estrategia para la Conservación y el Uso Sustentable de la Biodiversidad de la Ciudad de México (ECUSBE-CDMX) y su Plan de Acción al 2030 establece las medidas prioritarias para conservar su riqueza biológica y mantener los servicios ecosistémicos de los cuales depende el bienestar de sus habitantes. La Estrategia es una herramienta que la sociedad y el gobierno conocen y usan para incidir en las decisiones públicas, sociales y privadas, además de promover la transversalidad y la participación corresponsable de todos los actores y fomentar una cultura para la conservación y el uso sustentable de la biodiversidad en la Ciudad de México y su entorno regional.Esta Estrategia está conformada por seis ejes estratégicos: Conocimiento; Educación, comunicación y cultura; Conservación y restauración; Atención a los factores de presión; Manejo y uso sustentable; Transversalidad, participación y gobernanza, así como 80 acciones. En la Ciudad de México se ejecutó durante 2019 y 2024 (periodo de la administración pasada), el Programa Ambiental y de Cambio Climático, que es parte integral de nuestra política de desarrollo. El objetivo fue mejorar las condiciones ambientales en todas sus dimensiones, crear resiliencia y mitigar las emisiones de carbono con base en la innovación, la ciencia y la tecnología, y con la participación de la ciudadanía. Creemos que el bienestar de las personas solo es posible si hacemos una transición equitativa y sostenible, por ello nos apegamos a siete ejes estratégicos:
1. Revegetación campo y ciudad
2. Manejo sustentable del agua 
3. Rescate de ríos y cuerpos de agua
4. Basura Cero
5. Movilidad integrada y sustentable 
6. Calidad del aire
7. Ciudad Solar.

Administrativamente, el Programa culminó en diciembre del 2024, no obstante algunas de las acciones que se implementaron en sus ejes van a continuar como parte del Programa de Acción Climática de la Ciudad de México.

Con la implementación de este Programa, la Ciudad de México logró reducir de manera anual, alrededor de 2,300,000 ton de dióxido de carbono equivalente, logrando superar la meta de reducción de emisiones establecidas, dando cumplimiento del 105.5% de la meta.

In 2024, the City of Paris significantly updated its Land Use Plan (Plan Local d'Urbanisme or PLU) in order to align urban planning and construction laws with its environmental ambitions and the targets of its Climate Action Plan.

On top of protecting areas, anticipating future parks and general sustainability orientations and principles guiding constructions, it sets building obligations and recommendations that all construction permit must adhere to in order to be approved by the City. The PLU consequentially impacts both new and existing buildings, and strongly questions practices in order to ensure alignment with future climatic needs. Such guidelines include but are not limited to :

- Performance thresholds strengthening national regulations, of heat, cold and lighting needs, of primary energy consumption including non renewable, of construction footprint (580 kgeqCO2/m² for residential and 710 for offices), of yearly hours of uncomfortable heat (625 and 500 respectively, half of the current regulation), as well as a building vegetization index. All global renovations (>25% of the building value) must meet set energy performance thresholds and all roof or facade refection must aim to improve energy performance, allowing to exceed width, height and sidewalk encroaching of 30cm for exterior insulation, or 3m for sarking. Facade renovations must also preserve or add sun protections to exposed windows.

- District heating, to which all new buildings or buildings changing their collective heating, must connect to, within a delimited priority zone set in 2022. (The district heating, which main energy source is waste valorisation, has the long term contractual target to reach 100% renewable energy). 

- Renewables, which production or recuperation must be integrated to any new building or heavy renovation project unless technically or patrimonial wise impossible, allowing to exceed building height limits.

- Vegetalization, free land space must improve ecological qualities. Certain trees and green spaces are protected, and any tree must preferably be kept. If a cutting is justified, it must be compensated by an equivalent planting within the area.
 
The legislative document is accompanied by a series of guides and pedagogical ressources in order to facilitate appropriation of its implications, including a specific guide regarding environmental obligations and concerns. (https://cdn.paris.fr/paris/2025/07/17/250715_guideenvironnemental-tfz6.pdf)

The third Parisian Biodiversity Plan since 2011 was adopted in 2025, setting 20 additional targets and 85 actions.

In the face of climate change the protection and enhancement of biodiversity are crucial for our collective future. Biodiversity is not simply a list of species or genes but a living fabric of interconnectedness where the structure function and dynamics are as important as the composition itself. The strength of this fabric with diverse and functioning ecosystems is essential in both combating and adapting to climate change. Biodiversity serves as an indispensable pillar for the resilience of our territories. Paris takes pride in its biodiversity situated at a natural biogeographical crossroads where regional wildlife and flora can thrive. 

As such the Biodiversity is interconnected with the Climate Action Plan, sharing and implementing targets and nature priorities. Amongst which but not limited to :

- Exceeding 500 linear meters of middle vegetation stratas and each of the 20 city districts, by opening concrete and planting strips of bushes inbetween trees and where vegetation is lacking. 

- Ensuring an access to natural areas for every school, by generalizing 'oasis courtyards' and vegetated 'school streets (pedestrianized streets around or in front of schools)

- Create 500 new vegetated and pedestrianized streets in all of Paris (as approved by local referendum the 23rd of March 2025). 

- Vegetalization of an additional 40 hectares of rooves and facades, as well as the renaturation of 100 condominiums through the Copr'Oasis program.

- Renaturalizing the two main parisian woods, by increasing their diversity and density.

- Renaturalizing the Seine shores where possible, and increasing the presence of water within the city, by way of ponds and basins.

- Strentghen biodiversity within planning by way of the Biodiv'score, a project biodiversity assessment tool, developed by the city and to be used for its operations.

Pursuant to the Loi d'orientation des mobilités of 26 December 2019, the City of Paris officially adopted its Local Mobility Plan (PLM) in July 2025, which is the Parisian version of the Île-de-France Urban Travel Plan (PDUIF) currently in force and the Île-de-France Mobility Plan in project. 

It identifies four major stakes : decarbonization of mobilities, sobriety of travels, adapting the public space and transit offer for better inclusivity and accessibility, and protecting all parisians by adapting public space to extreme weather events. As such it articulates its goals and targets with the Climate Action Plan, with a heavy focus on reducing car dependency in infrastructures in favor of walking, sobriety in travel and collective transport. 

Among its actions and targets, the PLM notably expects :
- to triple bike travel that concern Paris, compared to 2020, which would represent an overall modal share of 13% (including long range, for which bike travel represents 3% of travels). This target goes alongside the Climate Action Plan aim to strengthen cycling infrastructures and to actualize the cycling plan in order to anticipate a 25% modal share of cycling for inner travel.

- a reduction by half of car travel within Paris by 2030 compared to 2015 levels, following current trends. This scenario is structural to City planning and the Climate Action Plan, which targets a reduction of public parking by half (-60 000) and to close streets to car travel, as an evolution of the share of public space allotted to private cars, in favor of pedestrianization and vegetalization (through the increase of school streets, garden streets, pedestrian hearts and urban forests). The Climate Action Plan, alongside the Biodiversity Plan and the Land Use Plan, aims a long term 40% of the territory to be made permeable (by 2050), which necessarily questions the amount of space allocated to car travel in the densest city of Europe. 

- The creation of a limited trafic zone in the center of Paris, which took effect November 5th 2024. Under current regulations, no private cars are allowed to drive within the perimeter without a legitimate reason (professionals, taxis, emergencies, accessibility reason, etc...). The goal is to give priority to walking and cycling within the area, as well as to forbid motorized vehicles crossing the dense zone without reasons to stop within. Municipal police controls have been progressively implemented starting 2025.

col8_Comment: The Plan de déplacements de l'administration parisienne (PDAP) aims to improve the mobility of its employees and travel linked to municipal activities (logistics, waste collection...) by encouraging the least polluting and most energy-efficient modes of transport (travel being the source of almost 20% of total greenhouse gas emissions and 9% of the administration's energy consumption). A pioneer in this field, the City of Paris has already switched its entire fleet of refuse collection vehicles from diesel to gas. In 2023, the City adopted its third PDAP for the period 2024-2030. While previous plans focused on de-dieselization, electrification of the municipal fleet, and encouraging more virtuous travel practices, PDAP3 will pursue these objectives and go further by placing the goal of decarbonization at the center. By 2030, the city is committed to phasing out the use of internal combustion engines for its vehicle fleet, with an initial target of 50% of the fleet using low-carbon or low-emission vehicles by 2026. In addition, it will gradually reduce the number of vehicles in its fleet, notably by developing shared-use solutions and promoting active mobility. For technical vehicles for which there are no electric alternatives, the City will turn to the use of bioGNV, derived from the methanization of food waste, or biofuels. The systematic replacement of gasoline-powered sidewalk cleaning machines (light vehicles) by electric machines, with a 100% electric fleet, will be achieved by 2026. As the market matures, the gradual switchover to collection with electric tippers will be undertaken, and will go hand in hand with the necessary electrification of garages and adaptation of their power supplies.

The first Parisian Environmental Health Plan (PPSE 1), passed in 2015, laid the foundations for protecting the health of Parisians through their environment. It was the subject of a review and revision, launched in March 2023 during the Environmental Health Conference (Assises de la Santé Environnementale). In November 2024, the Council of Paris adopted its second Parisian Environmental Health Plan (PPSE 2), in order to accelerate the policies and actions protecting Parisians through their daily lives and their environment. In order to take into account a rapidly evolving field (notably disease wise), the City established a Scientific and Citizen Council to exchange regularly, on the steering of the plan, its state, and the potential course corrections and changes required.

This second Plan builds on the progress made over the past seven years and a reflection on persistent and emerging needs in environmental health, such as climate change, emerging diseases, and new pollutants. It is also the result of eighteen months of consultation with institutional and grassroots stakeholders, as well as residents. It embodies a demanding ambition for the health of Parisians, is based on solid scientific knowledge, and addresses the still-profound social and territorial inequalities. As all city plan and strategies, it was conceived with a particular attention the Climate Action Plan targets and trajectories. It is built around three key principles:
- Fighting territorial and environmental social inequalities in health
- Taking priority action during the most sensitive periods of life, particularly during a child's first 1,000 days
- Relying on residents, stakeholders, and scientific experts to ensure that actions are as effective and relevant as possible

Drawing on citizens' experiences and incorporating new scientific knowledge in environmental health, it proposes 45 actions to enable Parisians to be born, grow, and age in good health, to breathe in a peaceful environment, to eat better, move around better, take better care of themselves, and to take easy action to improve what in their environment and daily lives is beneficial to their health, including in their homes. It also aims to put health into all policies, for example, so that all urban projects integrate health concerns from the design stage in the context of climate change, based on One Health approach, focusing on the interdependency of plants, nature and human health.

col8_Comment: In order to realize Taipei City's vision of a \'livable and sustainable\' city, the Department of Economic Development of Taipei City Government has been working on a new vision and development strategy for Taipei City's future industries since 2019. In the post-pandemic era, the industry needs to learn to live with more uncertainties, and how to make the best use of emerging technologies to build a competitive advantage and create a more resilient development model is an important issue for business operations and even city governance. At this time of rapid changes in the external environment, the \'Taipei City 2030 Future Industrial Development Policy White Paper \' (this White Paper) is presented as a demonstration of the government's proactive approach to the future industrial development of Taipei City.This White Paper is the collective wisdom of experts from various fields of industry, government, academia, and research, and we propose three key directions for the future industrial development of Taipei City - smart living, healthy living, and a sustainable environment. Under the three key directions, seven key development industries are proposed: A smart retail industry, a convention and exhibition industry, the tourism industry, a digital content industry, a smart health industry, a smart energy industry, and a circular design industry. Industrial development is an important key to building a happy life for citizens, and it is expected to create a positive cycle between industrial development and a \'livable and sustainable\' city, i.e., promoting the development of emerging industries, helping industries create added value, creating quality jobs, and generating government tax revenue, so that the government can continuously optimize the environment for industrial development.In the future, the Government will use the industrial projects planned in this White Paper to promote the future development of industries in Taipei City with the policy guidelines of \'from the inside to the outside\' and \'from public sector to private sector\', and make good use of the existing policy resources to pragmatically promote the development of industries in Taipei City, so as to make Taipei City a model city for the flourishing development of industries and a gateway to national trade and commerce.

col8_Comment: From 2003 to 2004, Taipei City Government began to develop the \'Integrated Water Management Plan\'.The main goal of the integrated water management plan is to reduce flooding and improve the overall capacity of the drainage system by taking measures through the proposed actionable items of integrated water management, such as sewer storage sharing, flood control pond sharing, watershed outflow suppression facility sharing, and drainage system improvement to ensure that drainage facilities meet the 5-year recurrence period storm drainage protection standard. Water retentionis then promoted through river basin sharing to provide a margin when the rainfall exceeds the drainage standards.In 2015, Taipei City Government further promoted the sponge city policy to bring the urban water environment to a new level, based on its long-standing promotion of \'integrated water management\' for urban flood-resisting and safety. The sponge city policy outlines the future vision of Taipei City with \'resilient water adaptation\', \'sustainable water use\', and \'friendly water environment”. The policy is based on six major goals, namely, \'sound urban water circulation\', \'improved flood-resisting capacity\', \'diversified and active water use\', \'stable and efficient water supply\', \'ecologically diverse water habitats\', and \'enriched and attractive water recreation” as the direction for the campaign. Finally, the policy adopts twelve promotion strategies, including \'water permeability and greening of public facilities\', \'water permeability and greening of private sector buildings\', \'urban river basin measures\', \'public-private partnership for intelligent disaster prevention\', \'wastewater recycling\', \'rainwater and groundwater utilization\', \'sound water supply system for catchment management\', \'water efficiency improvement\', \'environmental restoration of wetlands\', \'water quality improvement of rivers and streams\', \'water-friendly construction of rivers and streams\' and \'promotion of water activities along the riverbanks\' , which are taken as the implementation goals. Through engineering, management, and legal measures, and incorporating the concepts of open government, public participation, and public-private collaboration, the City Government will develop relevant promotion strategies and implementation plans, which will be implemented and promoted by various agencies of the City Government to jointly build Taipei into a safe, sustainable, and ecological sponge city.

col8_Comment: The ABB Air Quality Management Plan (AQMP) sets time-bound targets for key pollutants (PM2.5, PM10, NO₂, O₃) aligned with WHO 2021 guideline trajectories and national limit values. The plan inventories emissions from transport, buildings (heating/cooking), industry, construction dust, waste burning, and agriculture, then prioritizes measures with clear implementers, budgets, and timelines. Core measures include: (i) transport—bus fleet electrification, low-emission zones around the urban core, expansion of EV charging and active mobility networks; (ii) buildings—district heating decarbonization, accelerated boiler replacement to high-efficiency heat pumps, and energy-efficiency retrofits targeting low-income households; (iii) dust & construction—mandatory site enclosures, wheel-wash and paved access, real-time PM monitoring at major sites; (iv) waste—open burning ban enforcement, organics collection scale-up, landfill gas capture; and (v) industry—tightened NOx controls and solvent management (VOCs). Monitoring is conducted via fixed reference-grade stations supplemented by certified low-cost sensors for neighborhood coverage; data quality is assured through routine calibration and co-location. Public reporting occurs on a city dashboard and annual AQMP progress note; indicators track annual mean PM2.5/NO₂, days exceeding 24-h guidelines, source-attribution shares, and exposure of vulnerable groups (schools/health facilities). Co-benefits include reduced GHGs, road safety gains, energy savings, and health benefits quantified using standard exposure-response functions. The plan integrates with ABB's climate plan (mitigation/adaptation), SUMP, and building-energy codes to avoid trade-offs (e.g., biomass use where it would raise PM). Governance: Environment Dept. leads; Transport, Energy, Health, and Police support; a stakeholder forum (citizens, NGOs, academia, business) meets semi-annually. Financing blends municipal budget, national air-quality and energy-efficiency programs, and potential international grants. Risk & equity: actions are sequenced to prioritize hotspots and low-income districts; compliance support (e.g., scrappage/retrofit vouchers) is included. col8_Comment:
The vision for Cape Town is to deliver a clean city for all, where residents and businesses have access to quality, sustainable, and affordable waste services. To activate this vision, the City of Cape Town has collated its first Waste Strategy to navigate the significant challenges it faces in managing waste due to rapid urbanisation, population growth, increasing consumption patterns, and pervasive illegal dumping/littering.
 
The Waste Strategy, adopted by Council in May 2025, is built on three commitment pillars:
1. Optimising existing services - improving efficiencies within existing services
2. Minimising waste to landfill - making waste reduction easy and part of the culture of Cape Town
3. Maximising the basket of service offerings - expanding services through partnerships and tailoring
The Waste Strategy prioritises partnerships with key stakeholders in the waste industry including residents to address illegal dumping and reduce waste that ends up in landfill. It also highlights key actions to respond to waste challenges such as developing a plan for an additional landfill site, collaborating innovatively with waste generators and Producer Responsibility Organisations (PRO's) to minimise waste, and extending waste services to indigent backyard tenants on private property.

The waste strategy was launched on the 17 July 2025 and is available here: https://resource.capetown.gov.za/documentcentre/Documents/City strategies, plans and frameworks/CCT_Waste_Strategy.pdf

col3_Name of plan and URL link, if appli: City of Cape Town Energy Strategy: \n\nhttps://resource.capetown.gov.za/documentcentre/Documents/City%20strategies%2C%20plans%20and%20frameworks/Energy_Strategy.pdf
col5_Boundary of plan relative to jurisd: Same - covers entire jurisdiction and nothing else
col8_Comment:
The Energy Strategy sets out the City's vision and a programme of action to address the current national energy supply crisis while navigating the energy transition to the benefit of residents, businesses, and the environment for future generations. It has been developed to ensure that Cape Town can harness the opportunities available in a changing energy system, in partnership with residents and businesses. The strategy takes a system-wide perspective on energy, which means not only looking at electricity, for which the City currently has a significant mandate, but also engaging on broader energy-related matters over time.

The overarching vision for 2050 is Energy Security for a prosperous Cape Town. This vision is underpinned by four principles that describe the kind of energy system Cape Town needs - a resilient energy system that can provide reliable, affordable, and carbon-neutral energy to everyone living and working in Cape Town.
The application of the principles ensures that short-term priorities are implemented in such a way as to achieve, and not undermine, longer-term objectives. For example, the City is increasing electricity supply from alternative sources, predominantly renewable energy, which represents a significant investment towards a carbon-neutral energy system for Cape Town even in the short term, while also contributing to mitigating load-shedding and ensuring a reliable energy supply.

The Energy Strategy vision is implemented through three commitments and two cross-cutting enablers, namely:

•Commitment 1: Harness new energy supply
•Commitment 2: Alleviate Energy Poverty
•Commitment 3: Optimise Energy Use
•Enabler 1: Operate a future-fit utility business
•Enabler 2: Action by residents, businesses and partners

With the 2050 view on enabling, navigating, and driving changes within the energy system, the changes occurring in the different parts of the energy landscape will start to have an impact on the energy system as a whole, with the City's direct intervention in this transformation being achieved over three time- horizons:

•Short Term (by 2026): Increase capabilities to mitigate up to 4 stages of load-shedding
•Medium Term (by 2031): Transition to a financially sustainable electricity utility with enhanced operations and asset management practices
•Long Term (by 2050): Transforming the energy system to be carbon neutral

The Energy Strategy was approved in Oct 2023, followed by the development of 5 year Implementation plan.

The City of Cape Town's Integrated Public Transport Network (IPTN) Plan 2032 encourages a shift to more sustainable / efficient modes of transport for the 2032 horizon. Work is currently underway to update the IPTN Plan, which will guide the roll-out, or strengthening, of public transport corridors, with the update expected to be completed in 2026. The updated IPTN Plan will identify high priority public transport corridor projects consisting of key infrastructure and operations on certain road segments, ensuring a resilient and efficient public transport system capable of accommodating future passenger demand. These strategic transport investments ensure investments are precisely targeted where they are most needed to enhance connectivity and efficiency in an attempt to make mobility more affordable to passengers. The infrastructure projects could consist of a range of interventions from dedicating existing road space to public transport, construction of bus ways, stops, stations, rail networks and supporting infrastructure. 

The IPTN is to be updated every five years to account for updated transport data and behaviour, updated transport demand modelling and business planning, land use changes and alignment with corporate, provincial and national plans and strategies.

col8_Comment:
The City of Cape Town developed its first generation Air Quality Management Plan (AQMP) in 2005 that aimed to ensure that clean air is achieved and maintained in the City over the next 10 to 20 years. The City also developed various iterations of its Air Quality Management Bylaw to implement the policy and regulation various aspects of air quality (most recently amended in 2021). 

Based on nearly two decades of learning and actively striving to improve overall air quality in the City, a review of the AQMP was initiated in 2023 and the updated plan was formally adopted in March 2024. The overall objective of the plan is to strive for an environment where there is excellent air quality in all areas of Cape Town, and health impacts of air pollution due to poor air quality are mitigated through the goals set out in the AQMP, including: 

• GOAL 1: Reduce harmful greenhouse gas emissions through supporting air quality and climate change response programmes 
• GOAL 2: Ensure effective and consistent air quality management, linked to climate change response 
• GOAL 3: Raise awareness with respect to air quality management and climate change response 
• GOAL 4: Increase compliance through effective and consistent air quality compliance, monitoring and enforcement

Notable achievements include:
-The implementation of a diesel vehicle emissions testing program in partnership with the City's Traffic Services where in excess of 8000 vehicles are tested annually, by three diesel vehicle emissions testing teams.

-Compliance and enforcement activities are ongoing, with compliance and enforcement investigations of Licensed Listed Activities in terms of the Air Quality Act in order to ascertain compliance with Atmospheric Emission Licence conditions of authorisation and compliance with prescribed minimum emission standards. Administrative fines have been issued to unauthorised listed activities, with one operator paying a fine of R2 000 000.00 to regularise the unauthorised Listed Activity.

-Emission inventory development is an ongoing process, with new fuel burning equipment operators being permitted and regulated through the application of the City's Air Quality Management Bylaws. The City has a total of 1386 small fuel burning equipment appliances registered in the emission inventory.

-100% of our listed activities reported their Annual Atmospheric Emissions Inventories in terms of the applicable reporting regulations.

The Water Strategy sets out the City's high-level vision and plan for transitioning Cape Town to become “a water-sensitive city that optimises and integrates the management of water resources to improve resilience, competitiveness, and liveability for the prosperity of its people”. It outlines the importance of addressing climate change through integrating climate risk into water management planning and considering changes in rainfall, temperature and wind, and a likely increase in the intensity and frequency of extreme weather events. The Cape Town Water Strategy will be reviewed regularly as part of the formal Water Services Development Plan annual review process. The implementation of the strategy is monitored through existing planning instruments. Public engagement takes place through existing processes linked to the City's Integrated Development Plan and the Water Services Development Plan. The Water Strategy aims to ensure that the City prioritise collaborative processes to continue work with key stakeholders and partners, including other urban and agriculture water users and other spheres of government, to ensure that opportunities maximise economic, social and ecological benefits of regional water resources, and to reduce the risks.

Regarding the “Boundary of plan relative to jurisdiction boundary” selection, please see explanation: Currently, the City's main water supply comes from the Western Cape Water Supply System (WCWSS) which is a combination of 6 dams serving the City and surrounding smaller towns and agricultural irrigators. The system consists of infrastructure components owned and operated by both the City of Cape Town and the National Department of Water and Sanitation. Due to different regions involved including dependency on National Department of Water and Sanitation for decision making, the City's Water Strategy considers various stakeholders and neighbouring regions that will be impacted by decisions involving the WCWWS.

Comprehensive Integrated Transport Plan (CITP), 2023-2028

https://resource.capetown.gov.za/documentcentre/Documents/City%20strategies,%20plans%20and%20frameworks/CITP_2023-2028.pdf 

CITP 2024 Annual Update report: https://resource.capetown.gov.za/documentcentre/Documents/City%20strategies%2c%20plans%20and%20frameworks/CITP_2024_Annual_Update.pdf
col5_Boundary of plan relative to jurisd: Same - covers entire jurisdiction and nothing else
col8_Comment:
The National Land Transport Act (Act 5 of 2009) requires that a metropolitan municipality develops and updates its Comprehensive Integrated Transport Plan (CITP) for its area of jurisdiction. The City developed and approved a new CITP (2023 - 2028) in 2023, which sets out the plan towards the delivery of an integrated, intermodal and interoperable transport system and its related road and rail network. The CITP 2023 - 2028 guides the priorities and activities of the City's Urban Mobility Directorate in support of the following vision: All people should have efficient access to a range of opportunities in a manner that is sustainable and provides dignity. It is updated annually where necessary - latest available update is 2024 (see link provided). The annual update reports on new information, latest thinking, and changes in plans, projects, programmes and budgets from the previous year's progress of the implementation of the CITP.

In addition to alignment to the City's Integrated Development Plan, the CITP also aligns with the Municipal Spatial Development Framework and the Integrated Transport Network (IPTN) Plan in terms of the identified and prioritised development corridors. The corridors provide opportunities for land use intensification and an efficient movement system according to the principles of the Transit Oriented Development (TOD) Strategy. The CITP 2018 - 2023 indicates how the City intends to - over time - create an integrated transport system; address spatial integration to improve the sustainability and efficiency of public transport services; lower the cost of travelling; and reduce commuting time for residents.

Further to the above, work is underway to review and refine the transport objectives of the CITP as well as determining the desired outcomes in the short, medium and long terms. This is done through the development of a M&E framework for the CITP. The latest thinking on transport planning recognises and considers the impact of induced demand brought by road capacity expansion.

The CITP also provides the current status quo of transport services in Cape Town, from demand to supply, inclusive of all transport infrastructure such as roads, walk and cycle lanes, minibus-taxi facilities and public transport interchanges, MyCiTi bus facilities, stops and stations, as well as information about the current public transport services - the minibus-taxi routes, MyCiTi routes, rail lines, and so forth.

col8_Comment: The City of Cape Town High Heat Day and Heat Wave Action Plan, developed and approved by the City in 2023, consists of a portfolio of actions to be implemented in an integrated manner through the functions of multiple City of Cape Town departments responsible for the city's overall resilience, disaster risk management, health, occupational health and safety and various service delivery functions. The implementation of the plan aims to increase readiness for and reduce and prevent, risks to the public and the City's Business Continuity where possible. The Action Plan consists of two focus areas, including 11 actions that can be categorised as contributing to Heat Readiness (reducing the risk of heat events impacting the City's service delivery or business continuity) and Heat Response (responding to and managing various impacts of heat and the risk to the public shortly before and during a heat event) processes and functions. Heat related research, knowledge management and learning serves as a cross cutting function or pathway required to inform and support heat response and heat readiness decision-making and planning, in addition to contributing to monitoring and evaluation of this Plan.

col8_Comment:
The Municipal Spatial Development Framework (MSDF) is Cape Town's overarching long-term planning vision. It guides land use, urban form, growth management, infrastructure investments, and public/private development across the city. Additionally, the MSDF integrates district-level DSDFs (District Spatial Development Frameworks) and EMFs (Environmental Management Frameworks), which focus on local scale planning across Cape Town's eight planning districts. 

The MSDF aims to promote spatial transformation across Cape Town by addressing spatial inequality using spatially targeted approaches so that developments are beneficial to both Cape Town's citizens and its environment.

col5_Boundary of plan relative to jurisd: Same - covers entire jurisdiction and nothing else
col8_Comment: Estando conscientes do grande desafio que acompanha as mudanças climáticas nas cidades da América Latina, a Agência Francesa de Desenvolvimento (AFD) e o Banco de Desenvolvimento da América Latina (CAF) firmaram com a União Européia, um convênio de Facilitação de Investimentos para a América Latina (LAIF), que deu origem à iniciativa “Ciudades y Cambio Climático en América Latina”. Este convênio tem como objetivo a promoção do desenvolvimento de cidades com baixa emissão de carbono e resiliente às mudanças climáticas. Fortalecendo a sensibilização dos governos locais às mudanças climáticas e auxiliando na identificação e financiamento de projetos urbanos com co-benefícios climáticos.Em Fortaleza, o programa “Ciudades y Cambio Climático” teve o objetivo de estabelecer o Índice de Risco às Mudanças Climáticas na cidade de Fortaleza, considerando suas particularidades territoriais; e seu Plano de Adaptação, que identifica medidas concretas de adaptação, para reduzir a vulnerabilidade e aumentar a capacidade de resposta do município frente aos eventos extremos oriundos das mudanças climáticas aos quais verificou-se que a cidade está exposta.A construção dos documentos, Índice de Vulnerabilidade às Mudanças Climáticas (IVCC) e Plano de Adaptação de Fortaleza, foi realizada por equipe técnica composta por consórcio de 3 empresas. O processo de priorização das ações foi realizado de forma participativa, por meio de validação com mesa técnica formada por especialistas e representantes dos órgãos direta e indiretamente relacionados à temática em questão, organizações não governamentais, representantes da comunidade acadêmica e oficinas envolvendo as comunidades de áreas distintas do território de Fortaleza como instância de participação da sociedade civil.

col3_Name of plan and URL link, if appli: Política da Qualidade do Ar de Fortaleza https://urbanismoemeioambiente.fortaleza.ce.gov.br/urbanismo-e-meio-ambiente/766-monitoramento-da-qualidade-do-ar \n
col5_Boundary of plan relative to jurisd: Same - covers entire jurisdiction and nothing else
col8_Comment: A estação utilizada para o monitoramento, registra continuamente, hora a hora, 24 horas por dia, as concentrações dos parâmetros de qualidade do ar: Ozônio, Monóxido de Carbono, Monóxido de Nitrogênio, Dióxidos de Nitrogênio, Óxidos de Nitrogênio, Dióxido de Enxofre, Metano, Partículas Inaláveis Finas < 2,5 e μm Partículas Inaláveis < 10 μm. São monitorados, também, os parâmetros de meteorologia: Temperatura do Ar, Umidade Relativa do Ar, Pressão Atmosférica, Radiação Solar, Velocidade e Direção do Vento e Precipitação Pluviométrica.Os Relatórios de Monitoramento apresentam os resultados do monitoramento, realizado por mês, da Estação Móvel de Monitoramento da Qualidade do Ar. Este monitoramento é realizado em consonância com as diretrizes estabelecidas na Resolução CONAMA n° 491 de novembro de 2018. O método de avaliação envolve as medições das concentrações de ozônio (O3), monóxido de carbono (CO), dióxidos de nitrogênio (NO2), dióxidos de enxofre (SO2), partículas inaláveis (PM2,5 e PM10). \n\nPor fim, vale destacar ainda, o lançamento da política de vigilância da qualidade do ar em maio de 2023. Com a política, a capital cearense, que antes contava apenas com a Estação Móvel de Qualidade do Ar (EMQAR) da SEUMA, passou a contar com uma rede de 25 monitores de baixo custo, ampliando a rede de monitoramento da qualidade do ar do município.

col3_Name of plan and URL link, if appli: La Guía para la Gobernanza y Resiliencia Metropolitana (2024): https://drive.google.com/file/d/1TaIHyUdr5uWyujtQ1z-XRAE5GeP3HT--/view
col5_Boundary of plan relative to jurisd: Same - covers entire jurisdiction and nothing else
col8_Comment:
Es una iniciativa desarrollada por las áreas metropolitanas de Barcelona (AMB) y Guadalajara (AMG), con el apoyo financiero de la Unión Europea, a través de la Acción Metro Resilience Guadalajara (MRG).
Esta Guía busca proponer un modelo de referencia para fortalecer la resiliencia
metropolitana, con base en la experiencia y conocimientos generados por ambas
metrópolis, e inspirar a otros gobiernos locales a integrar la resiliencia y emprender
acciones a escala metropolitana; alineadas con la Nueva Agenda Urbana (Hábitat III) y la Agenda 2030 para el Desarrollo Sostenible, en particular con el objetivo de desarrollo sostenible (ODS) 11: “Hacer que las ciudades y los asentamientos humanos sean inclusivos, seguros, resilientes y sostenibles”.

Además, a partir de las lecciones aprendidas en la implementación de la Acción MRG, se identifican factores clave para promover cambios significativos en los modelos metropolitanos de gobernanza, e impulsar prácticas más colaborativas y sostenibles.

La Guía combina la experiencia de dos metrópolis líderes en resiliencia, para ofrecer una perspectiva global y comparativa. Se apoya, además, en una revisión del estado del arte, análisis documental y referencias internacionales, para complementar el conocimiento generado entre ambas metrópolis, y recupera los aprendizajes y el
diálogo generado a partir del Congreso Internacional de Resiliencia Metropolitana, un espacio que reunió a más de 20 especialistas de cinco continentes, comprometidos con la resiliencia y la gobernanza metropolitana.

La Guía está dirigida a personas involucradas en los procesos de toma de decisiones
y responsables del diseño y ejecución de políticas públicas, y busca convertirse en
un instrumento de colaboración y transferencia de conocimientos entre metrópolis
alrededor del mundo.
