col3_Name of plan and URL link, if appli: Sunderland Core Strategy and Development Plan (CSDP), available at https://www.sunderland.gov.uk/CSDP
col5_Boundary of plan relative to jurisd: Same - covers entire jurisdiction and nothing else
col8_Comment:
The CSDP sets out citywide development plans to 2033 and has policies that reflect Sunderland's environmental sustainability ambitions.
The CSDP has a spatial vision that Sunderland will be at the heart of a low carbon regional economy. Policy WWE1 ensures that the development of decentralised, renewable, and low carbon energy will be supported. Policy BH1 requires development to achieve high-quality design standards and maximise opportunities to create sustainable mixed-use developments and for the use of sunlight/solar energy. Policy BH2 requires the incorporation of sustainable design and construction methods, maximising efficient and clean energy.
Policies WWE2&3 aim to reduce flood risk and implement sustainable coastal management. Policy NE1 states development should apply climate change mitigation and adaptation measures, including flood and watercourse management.
Policy WWE4 aims to enhance water security, by requiring the quantity and quality of water bodies to be protected, and enhanced. It also requires developments that discharge into a watercourse to incorporate pollution control measures, and developments which run nearby a watercourse to consider opportunities to improve river environments and water quality.
Policy WWE6 requires development to support waste minimisation, re-use and recovery.
Policy BH2 requires major development to include opportunities to enhance biodiversity. Policy NE1 seeks to protect the environment by maintaining and improving green and blue infrastructure. Policy NE2 ensures that development must demonstrate how it will provide biodiversity net gain and minimise adverse impacts on biodiversity in accordance with the mitigation hierarchy. It also aims to safeguard SSSIs, local wildlife sites, wildlife corridors and local nature reserves. Policy NE3 requires development to provide biodiversity net gain through woodlands, hedgerows and trees. Policy WWE4 ensures that development close to or in in a main river or ordinary watercourse should consider opportunities to improve the river environment and water quality by improving the biodiversity and ecological connectivity of the watercourse. SCC reviewed the CSDP in Dec 2024, which confirmed that whilst the policies remain fit-for purpose for decision making at that point in time, committed the Council to commencing the preparation of a new Local Plan utilising a more integrated approach. The Council's low carbon commitments will be reflected in the new Local Plan.

Riverside Sunderland is a new urban quarter being developed in Sunderland city centre. The Riverside Sunderland Masterplan has the ambition of developing Riverside Sunderland into one of the UK's first carbon-neutral neighbourhoods. Key goals of the Riverside Sunderland low emissions approach are to design for low energy consumption; maximise opportunities for heat recovery; integrate Riverside Sunderland into a city-wide low-carbon heating network; generate energy from renewable sources; reduce car dependency and use modern methods of construction (MMC).
A Supplementary Planning Document was adopted by the Council in December 2020 which provides planning guidance for the delivery of the site.

Regarding climate change mitigation, reducing energy consumption and using clean energy are key aspects of the Riverside Sunderland Masterplan. A range of targets for both domestic and non-domestic buildings are set out for both 2027 and 2033 to reduce operational energy, reduce space heating demand, increase renewable generation on roofs, reduce embodied carbon, and decrease potable water use. For example, the Riverside Sunderland project aims to reduce the operational energy consumption in domestic buildings to 70 kWh/m2/y by 2027, and to 0-35 kWh/m2/y by 2033.

Regarding climate change adaptation, the Riverside Sunderland SPD requires development to incorporate SuDS as integral features to the green infrastructure and street layout, to act as positive features to the development and help to reduce flood risk. Development is also required to ensure that surface water run-off levels are in accordance with council standards. The Riverside Sunderland Masterplan also ensures that tree planting and sustainable urban drainage will promote climate change resilience.

The Riverside Sunderland Masterplan is guided by principles of integrated sustainability and consequently, Riverside Sunderland aims to support a circular economy by using efficient designs, sustainable materials, and nature-based solutions, as well as working with the landscape to implement sustainable urban drainage.

Riverside Sunderland has been shortlisted for the Government Property Awards 2025 for the Transforming Places award.

col8_Comment:
One of the statutory functions of the Health and Wellbeing Board (HWB) is to prepare a Joint Strategic Needs Assessment (JSNA), working in collaboration with partners 
and the wider community, to identify the health and wellbeing needs of the local population. It provides an insight into current and future health, wellbeing and daily living needs of local people and informs the commissioning of services and interventions to improve health and wellbeing outcomes and reduce inequalities.

The findings of the JSNA are based on:
• Consideration of the JSNA topic summaries, which identify health, social care and wellbeing indicators, including the results of local Lifestyle Surveys;
• Comparison of our local population against regional and national averages and, in some cases, statistical neighbours which helps us to understand if a particular health issue is significant; and
• A summary of local needs analysis that has been carried out, identification of 
effective interventions (what works) and any other rationale for action e.g. a national 'must do' or service users', carers' and public views. 

This overarching JSNA provides a summary of the health needs of Sunderland and highlights relevant issues for the commissioning of services. Sunderland is using this insight to support the development of a climate change adaptation plan for the city - risks associated with climate change will affect residents in different ways and the understanding of population needs and vulnerabilities is crucial when assessing risk to inform adaptation.

Sunderland Green Infrastructure Delivery and Action Plan, available at https://www.sunderland.gov.uk/media/21396/EX1-017-Sunderland-Green-Infrastructure-Delivery-and-Action-Plan/pdf/EX1.017_Sunderland_Green_Infrastructure_-_Delivery_and_Action_Plan.pdf?m=636918745551330000

col8_Comment:
The Green Infrastructure Strategy was commissioned by Sunderland City Council to inform and support Sunderland's Core Strategy and Development Plan (CSDP) 2015-2033. It builds upon a wealth of work already conducted by the Council, in assessing the quality and quantity of greenspace provision in local neighbourhoods across the city and identifying a set of district and inter- district Green Infrastructure Corridors.

The importance of these Corridors in protecting and enhancing the existing GI assets that provide multiple benefits to people and wildlife across Sunderland is highlighted in this study. They define our settlements, whilst providing a connected landscape within which biodiversity, natural processes and ecosystem services can function. The natural capital we derive from these functions will become increasingly important to support sustainable growth alongside climate change and population expansion.

This study also builds upon the Council's Greenspace Audit and utilises a range of wider socioeconomic and environmental indicators, relevant to the NPPF's objectives, in order to map where there is greatest area-based need for the public benefits that GI brings. The evidence base is then combined in order to highlight where there is greatest potential for economic, social, environmental and multi-functional outcomes from green infrastructure interventions. The resulting maps provide an overview of where enhancements to promote GI could deliver the greatest benefits for wildlife and people.

The study recognises that certain indicators require further refinement and that the mapping outputs must be considered only as an aid to strategic planning. Local knowledge and conditions; political and community values; ownership, partnerships, access and stewardship are all amongst further factors which must be considered and brought to bear in order to sustainably enhance and connect GI appropriately across the City.

Finally, a set of priorities is defined for GI delivery in Sunderland with a summary of recommended next steps to take the strategy forward. These will be co-ordinated across the Council ensuring an integrated approach in relation to green infrastructure.

https://www.sunderland.gov.uk/media/28328/Local-Cycling-and-Walking-Infrastructure-Plan-SCC/pdf/oce22286_CoS_LCWIP_A4_NEW.pdf?m=638169218230370000
col5_Boundary of plan relative to jurisd: Same - covers entire jurisdiction and nothing else
col8_Comment:
The Local Cycling and Walking Infrastructure Plan (LCWIP) document, which was adopted by Cabinet in October 2022, explores walking and cycling in Sunderland and sets out a Local Cycling and Walking Infrastructure Plan (LCWIP). It provides a comprehensive framework to guide Sunderland City Council and its partners regarding planned walking and cycling infrastructure over the next 10 years. The plan is used to support funding applications to enable delivery and in taking planning and design decisions regarding transport schemes more broadly, including Active Travel which is specially walking and cycling.
The geographical scope of this LCWIP is the area within Sunderland City Council's boundary. The Council is also consulting and considering how Sunderland's network links to those of neighbouring authorities.

The LCWIP supports a local approach to delivering both the Government and City Council's ambitions to create a cycling and walking nation, as outlined in the Department for Transport's Cycling and Walking Strategy (2017) and will guide future cycling and walking developments in line with our shared walking and cycling ambitions. A draft Washington LCWIP is now completed, with consultation on the document planned for the Period September - October 2025. An area-focused LCWIP is now in production for the Coalfields area of Sunderland.
Sunderland has ambitious plans for growth and regeneration. With this in mind, Sunderland continues to look at the existing cycling network across the city, assess potential future routes and improve cross boundary links. The aim being to create a high-quality cycling network with signage across the city. Currently, an extensive programme of Cycling infrastructure investment is underway across the City. This will provide 16km of new high-quality facilities with an investment value of £23.2m.

col8_Comment: The Northumbrian Water Resources Management Plan 2021-2025 (WRMP - attached in section 14) and the Northumbria Water Basin Management Plan cover Sunderland and have water security targets. The WRMP aims to reduce leakage by 15% between 2020 and 2025, and a further 10% over each subsequent 5-year period through to 2045. In addition, the WRMP aims to annually reduce per capita water consumption by 0.12l/head/day (0.33 Ml/day) by delivering water efficiency activities. The Northumbria Water Basin Management Plan aims to provide a long-term framework to protect water quality within the river basin district. The plan has numerous objectives in-line with the European Water Framework Directive. The main environmental objectives are to prevent deterioration of surface and groundwater; achieve good status for all water bodies or, for heavily modified water bodies and artificial water bodies, good ecological potential and good surface water chemical status; reverse significant increases in the concentrations of pollutants in groundwater; and reduce discharges, emissions and losses of hazardous substances into surface water.

col8_Comment:
Flooding is the most significant climate hazard in Sunderland with coastal, river and surface water flooding all being hazards to residents and the economy as identified in the climate risk and vulnerability module. Furthermore, it is expected that the frequency and intensity of flooding events in the jurisdiction will increase in the event of 1.5°C global warming being exceeded.

Sunderland prepares a Local Flood Risk Management Strategy. The purpose of the LFRMS is to act as a robust guidance tool for Risk Management Authorities operating in Sunderland to deliver a coordinated, improved approach in all flood risk management activities. In addition, the overriding vision for the LFRMS is for Sunderland City Council to take a lead role in better understanding local flood risk. Providing this information in the form of the LFRMS will enable communities to also improve their own knowledge and understanding of the risk of flooding across Sunderland.
The LFRMS update is currently on hold due to changes in legislation (Flood and Water Management Act), therefore Sunderland Council is waiting for Defra to confirm dates of when these changes are going to take effect.

col3_Name of plan and URL link, if appli: Estudio Conceptual para Intervenciones en el\nmarco del proyecto 'Centro Histórico Bajo en\nEmisiones' en Cuenca
col5_Boundary of plan relative to jurisd: Other: Aplica para el Centro Histórico de la ciudad de Cuenca
col8_Comment:
El proyecto 'Centro Histórico bajo en emisiones' es un plan de movilidad urbana sostenible que busca reducir la contaminación ambiental, priorizando el transporte público eléctrico y la movilidad no motorizada en el centro histórico de la ciudad. Los principales componentes incluyen la expansión de la red de ciclovías, la adquisición de buses eléctricos para el sistema de transporte público y la creación de calles completas para peatones y transporte público. 
Objetivos principales
Mejorar la calidad de vida: Busca mejorar la habitabilidad de los ciudadanos y proteger el bienestar de las futuras generaciones a través de una ciudad más segura y limpia.
Proteger el patrimonio: Busca conservar el Centro Histórico, declarado Patrimonio de la Humanidad por la UNESCO, reduciendo el impacto ambiental de la movilidad.
Reducir emisiones de carbono: Se estima que el proyecto contribuirá a la reducción de emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero, considerando la alta dependencia del transporte de la ciudad. 
Componentes clave
Movilidad no motorizada: Se planea la expansión de 20 km de ciclovías y la implementación de estaciones de bicicleta pública con nuevas tecnologías.
Transporte público eléctrico: Se contempla la adquisición de buses eléctricos para el sistema de transporte público, complementado por el tranvía existente.
Calles completas: Se transformarán calles principales en 'calles completas' donde se dé prioridad a la circulación del transporte público y los peatones, limitando el espacio para vehículos privados y su velocidad.

O Manual de Boas Práticas é um documento orientador para as empresas do Concelho que pretendam implementar estratégias de sustentabilidade intensificando-se assim, a implementação de ferramentas de monitorização e otimização para o pleno cumprimento dos três pilares da sustentabilidade: económico, social e ambiental. O 'Plano Estratégico para o Desenvolvimento Sustentável 2030' do Município de Braga é um documento ambicioso que visa institucionalizar os Objetivos de Desenvolvimento Sustentável (ODS) da ONU, com o objetivo de melhorar a qualidade de vida dos cidadãos bracarenses. O plano abrange o período de 2023 a 2025 e propõe um conjunto de 10 ações estratégicas que serão implementadas em colaboração com a comunidade local e parceiros estratégicos.

As ações estão alinhadas com uma abordagem que envolve o envolvimento da comunidade, análise de megatendências e a criação de um modelo estratégico robusto. A participação da população é considerada essencial, e mecanismos de monitorização e avaliação foram estabelecidos para garantir a eficácia das medidas implementadas.

O plano foca em áreas prioritárias como mobilidade, habitação, gestão de água e desenvolvimento urbano sustentável, propondo um fortalecimento do Plano Diretor Municipal (PDM) e a promoção de políticas de incentivos sustentáveis. Também inclui a criação de um Laboratório de Inovação para fomentar o empreendedorismo sustentável e o estabelecimento de um Conselho Estratégico para o Desenvolvimento Sustentável, envolvendo especialistas e líderes comunitários.

O compromisso com a sustentabilidade é refletido na intenção de garantir que mais de 80% do Orçamento Municipal seja direcionado para projetos relacionados com os ODS, promovendo assim uma Braga mais inclusiva, resiliente e ambientalmente responsável. Através de uma implementação coordenada e integrada, o plano visa moldar um futuro sustentável para a cidade até 2030, alinhando-se com as prioridades globais enquanto respeita as necessidades locais.

The 'New Taipei City Autonomous Ordinance on Climate Change Response (Draft)', which will serve as the foundation for promoting net-zero transformation in the city, is currently being drafted and was submitted to the city council for review in 2022. Since net-zero transformation is a long-term undertaking requiring flexible adjustments based on implementation status and technological advancements, and sustained support for transition initiatives, the city government proposed four overarching principles in drafting the ordinance: 'integrated governance and flexible operation,' 'premium subsidies under the climate fund,' 'green financial investment market,' and 'ensuring both a just transition and continued development.'

'Integrated governance and flexible operation' means that the provisions are task-oriented, starting with an inventory of key transition projects and allocating responsibilities accordingly. If certain responsibilities remain undefined, the ordinance specifies the measures but allows implementation timelines, responsibilities, and applicable areas to be determined based on future scientific assessments. 'Premium subsidies under the climate fund' provide a legal basis for managing future central allocations of carbon fees to local governments and donations from companies that fail to achieve carbon neutrality. A transparent oversight mechanism can be established to support transformation efforts by communities, campuses, households, and businesses. The 'green financial investment market' aims to encourage listed and OTC companies of a certain scale in New Taipei City to disclose environmental information and guide the market toward eco-friendly practices. 'Ensuring both a just transition and continued development' is reflected in the ordinance by explicitly designating the climate fund for just transition purposes and recognizing behavior change as a key incentivized measure.

The main chapters of the current draft cover six key areas: urban and rural adaptation, building energy conservation and efficiency enhancement, circular economy and resource utilization, energy and industrial innovation, smart green transportation, and promotion of zero-carbon education and lifestyles. Additional chapters include general provisions, penalties, and supplementary clauses, providing a robust legal foundation in terms of scope, definitions, and tools for implementation.

The city plans to use the implementation experience gained from this demonstration district as a foundation to expand carbon reduction efforts and climate change adaptation work across the entire city.

Currently, greenhouse gas emissions in Bali District are primarily generated by the industrial sector, accounting for 42%, followed by the residential and commercial sectors at 30%, and the transportation sector at 28%. With the rapid development of industry and commerce, electricity consumption in the district continues to rise. To address this, the city will promote three major strategies and five key directions to transform Bali into a net-zero carbon demonstration area.

The three core strategies include gradually phasing out fossil fuels, improving the energy efficiency of equipment, and increasing the use of clean and renewable energy. Beyond carbon reduction, climate change adaptation efforts will also be strengthened to create a high-quality living environment in which people and nature can coexist in harmony. The Bali District Disaster Response Center will be responsible for managing various disaster response actions. Special attention will be given to vulnerable groups, particularly elderly residents of the Bali Nursing Home and low-income households, by conducting risk assessments and developing appropriate response measures, ensuring that no one is left behind in the transition process.

The purpose of the Bacolod City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Plan (BDRRMP) is to reduce disaster risks and their impacts on the city and its residents. This is not solely the responsibility of the city government, but a collaborative effort involving barangay units, civil society organizations, the private sector, and other government agencies.

Mainstreaming DRRM: Integrating disaster risk reduction and climate change adaptation into local development policies, plans, and budgets.

Preparedness: Conducting various trainings and drills for disaster preparedness in schools and homes, including emergency and earthquake drills.

Response: Providing 24/7 emergency medical and response services.

Mitigation: Implementing projects like flood control programs.

Inclusivity: Ensuring that disaster management initiatives are inclusive, with specific attention to women, children, and people with disabilities. This includes having sex, age, and disability-disaggregated data, and making public spaces and drills accessible.

Monitoring and Evaluation: Establishing a system to monitor and evaluate the plan's implementation, using feedback to improve future activities and better achieve local goals.

Legal Compliance: Ensuring that the plan and its implementation adhere to national laws, such as Republic Act No. 10121, also known as the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010.

col5_Boundary of plan relative to jurisd: Same - covers entire jurisdiction and nothing else
col8_Comment:
Cagayan de Oro City's 10-Year Solid Waste Management (SWM) Plan, approved by the National Solid Waste Management Commission (NSWMC) in 2018, has served as the city's blueprint for addressing waste generation, segregation, collection, and disposal in compliance with Republic Act 9003. Since its approval, the plan has been implemented through the City Local Environment and Natural Resources Office (CLENRO) and the City Solid Waste Management Board, with enforcement anchored on the “No segregation, No collection” policy and strengthened ordinances. Major components of implementation included the safe closure and rehabilitation of the city's old dumpsite, the development of a sanitary landfill, the establishment of barangay-level Materials Recovery Facilities (MRFs), and the promotion of composting and recycling to reduce the volume of waste requiring final disposal. 

The plan also provided for improved collection systems, hazardous and medical waste management, and financing mechanisms to support capital investments and operational costs. Community engagement, education campaigns, and partnerships with barangays, private sector actors, and informal recyclers played a crucial role in achieving waste diversion targets and promoting behavioral change at the household level.

Now that the plan is due for updating, the city revisits its achievements and gaps, taking into account population growth, changing waste generation patterns, facility performance, and lessons learned from implementation. Updating the plan requires new waste data, a reassessment of landfill capacity and MRF operations, and a recalculation of investment requirements and diversion targets. Stakeholder consultations at the barangay and city levels, along with at least one public hearing, are also necessary to ensure inclusive participation. 

The revised plan must align with updated NSWMC guidelines, incorporate strategies to prevent and reduce marine litter, the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) to promote plastic circularity, greenhouse gas mitigation strategies and use emerging waste management technologies, and strengthen financing strategies, whether through city budget allocations, national government programs, or public-private partnerships.

col8_Comment:
The Council Plan has a top priority of continuing to deliver a healthier, clean and green Kirklees with a sustainable economy, and to address the challenges of climate change. There are four key partnership strategies that have been developed and delivered with partners across the district: 
•	Health and Wellbeing Strategy
•	Environment Strategy
•	Inclusive Communities Framework
•	Inclusive Economy Strategy
The key deliverables are to begin implementation of a new Environment Strategy setting out our borough's commitment and ambitious vision for greater action on environmental issues, whilst also addressing the ecological and climate emergencies. Support the role of our communities in looking after local environments and improving recycling behaviours. Support social interaction, volunteering and community groups in relation to the protection and greening of our environment as set out within the Environment Strategy. Continue to develop and begin delivery of a Parks and Greenspaces Strategy that will support the provision of welcoming, accessible and high-quality parks and greenspaces to allow people, business, nature and wildlife to flourish (Summer 2025). Play a leading role in the ongoing development of the Health and Care Plan, working with partners and communities to improve physical and mental health outcomes, paying particular attention to addressing inequalities in this area and promoting early intervention. Implementation of the 'The Big Plan', which will provide support to children and families with special educational needs and disabilities. Delivery of 'Year 1' of the action plan for the new Inclusion and Diversity Strategy. Supporting the local care market to be diverse, high quality and sustainable by ensuring there is quality support and accommodation for adults with complex requirements. This is being done by the opening Knowl Park House, with modern facilities, allowing for the support of people with complex dementia. Development of Phase 1 of the Cultural Heart, an ambitious centrepiece for Huddersfield and the whole of Kirklees, including a new library, food hall and events square. To produce, consult on and begin delivery of the Kirklees Transport Strategy, setting the vision and framework for the future transport network in Kirklees.

col5_Boundary of plan relative to jurisd: Same - covers entire jurisdiction and nothing else
col8_Comment: The Sustainable Transport Delivery Plan for Dundee sets out a comprehensive 10-year strategy to transform the city's transport infrastructure in alignment with national climate goals and evolving travel behaviours. It prioritises active travel, public transport, and shared mobility over private car use, aiming to reduce carbon emissions, improve air quality, and enhance accessibility for all residents. The plan is informed by Scotland's National Transport Strategy and the Regional Transport Strategy developed by Tactran, and it supports the national objective to reduce car kilometres by 20% by 2030.\n\nKey interventions include the development of “Active Freeways” (segregated walking, wheeling, and cycling corridors), expansion of electric vehicle charging infrastructure, implementation of 20mph zones and School Streets, and improvements to bus services and priority corridors. The plan also promotes Mobility as a Service (MaaS), integrated digital ticketing, and the creation of mobility hubs to facilitate multi-modal travel. With an estimated investment of £230 million, the strategy is designed to be adaptable to future technological and behavioural changes, and it positions Dundee as a leader in sustainable urban transport.

col8_Comment: The Flood Risk Management Plan (FRMP) for the Tay Estuary and Montrose Basin Local Plan District (LPD 7) outlines a strategic framework for managing flood risk across a diverse region that includes urban centres like Dundee, Montrose, and Arbroath, as well as rural and coastal areas. Covering approximately 2,700 km² and home to around 340,000 people, the plan identifies 15 Potentially Vulnerable Areas (PVAs) and sets out tailored objectives and actions for each. It addresses flood risks from rivers, surface water, and coastal sources, with projections indicating a significant increase in flood exposure by the 2080s due to climate change.\n\nThe plan includes a wide range of actions such as flood forecasting and warning improvements, infrastructure maintenance, natural flood management, and community engagement. It promotes adaptive planning and integrated catchment approaches, with collaboration between SEPA, local authorities, Scottish Water, and other stakeholders. Each PVA has its own set of proposed interventions, ranging from flood protection schemes and surface water management plans to shoreline management and resilience-building initiatives. The FRMP is part of a six-year planning cycle and is designed to evolve with new data, climate projections, and community feedback.

Program Ochrony Środowiska miasta Rzeszowa na lata 2025-2029 pełni zasadniczą

col8_Comment:
En junio de 2022 fue publicada en Chile la Ley Marco de Cambio Climático (Ley Nº 21.455, en adelante LMCC), en la que se establece un marco jurídico con el objetivo de convertir a Chile en un país carbono neutral y resiliente a los efectos del cambio climático al año 2050.

Para ello, la LMCC dispone de una serie de instrumentos de gestión del cambio climático, destinados a abordar tanto sus impactos negativos, como mitigar las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero. La Ley Marco dispone en su artículo 12 que “las municipalidades deberán elaborar planes de acción comunal de cambio climático, los que serán consistentes con las directrices generales establecidas en la Estrategia Climática de Largo Plazo y en los planes de acción regional de cambio climático”.

Estos planes, deben incluir una caracterización de la vulnerabilidad y potenciales impactos del cambio climático en la comuna; medidas de mitigación y adaptación a nivel comunal; una descripción detallada de las medidas que consideran, sus plazos de implementación, la asignación de responsabilidades y la identificación de sus fuentes de financiamiento, así como indicadores de monitoreo, reporte y verificación de cumplimiento de las medidas del Plan.

El PPDA es un instrumento de gestión ambiental que busca cumplir con las normas de calidad del aire en la Región Metropolitana en un horizonte de 10 años. Está enfocado en contaminantes críticos: material particulado grueso (MP10), material particulado fino (MP2,5), ozono (O₃) y monóxido de carbono (CO).

El plan combina medidas regulatorias y programáticas en calefacción residencial, transporte, industria y gestión territorial, además de acciones de educación ambiental y gestión de episodios críticos de contaminación para las comunas de la Región Metropolitana de Santiago, dentro de las que se encuentra la comuna de Peñalolén. Su fin es reducir emisiones, proteger la salud de la población y mejorar la calidad de vida, considerando los co-beneficios en mitigación del cambio climático (por ejemplo, reducción de carbono negro).

El PPDA fija metas normativas de calidad del aire, que deben alcanzarse progresivamente:

1) MP10 y MP2,5: Reducir concentraciones anuales y trianuales. Disminuir días y horas sobre la norma vigente. Bajar episodios de Preemergencia y Emergencia.

2) Ozono (O₃): Reducir concentraciones trianuales para el promedio de 8 horas.

3) Monóxido de carbono (CO): Cumplir con las normas de concentración anual y de 8 horas, que actualmente ubican a la RM en condición de latencia

col8_Comment:
El Plan de Reducción de Riesgos de Desastres (PRRD) de la comuna de Punta Arenas es un instrumento de planificación local que busca anticipar, prevenir y reducir los impactos de amenazas naturales y antrópicas sobre la población, la infraestructura y los ecosistemas. Este plan se enmarca en la Ley 21.364 de Gestión del Riesgo de Desastres y se articula con la Estrategia Nacional para la Reducción del Riesgo de Desastres, garantizando coherencia con los lineamientos regionales y nacionales.

En Punta Arenas, este instrumento cobra especial relevancia debido a su condición geográfica y climática, que la hace vulnerable a fenómenos como temporales de viento, marejadas, inundaciones costeras, nevazones, olas de frío extremo e incendios de interfaz urbano-rural. El plan no solo identifica estas amenazas, sino que también evalúa la exposición y vulnerabilidad de la población, proponiendo medidas de preparación y respuesta.

Asimismo, el PRRD se vincula directamente con el Plan de Acción Comunal de Cambio Climático (PACCC), ya que la variabilidad y el cambio climático incrementan la frecuencia e intensidad de algunos eventos de riesgo. De este modo, se asegura la integración entre gestión de riesgos y acción climática, permitiendo diseñar estrategias más efectivas de adaptación.

col8_Comment: The City of Canada Bay has joined over 1,000 local governments and jurisdictions worldwide to declare a climate emergency. The declaration was endorsed unanimously at the City of Canada Bay's September 17 Council meeting following a motion by Councillor Charles Jago. “We have a responsibility to our community and planet to not only reduce our greenhouse gas emissions but implement climate change mitigation and adaptation measures to safeguard the beautiful place we call home,” said Mayor Angelo Tsirekas. The declaration is consistent with the position of the NSW Government that councils are responsible for many services and assets likely to be affected by climate change and must take steps to prepare for and minimise its effects. The City of Canada Bay is the twelfth local government in Greater Sydney region to declare a climate emergency as part of the global movement. The declaration will see Council take action on the following five recommendations from Councillor Charles Jago's notice of motion: THAT Council recognises that we are in a state of climate emergency that requires urgent action by all levels of government, including local councils and that by taking urgent action it is still possible to prevent the most catastrophic outcomes. THAT Building on actions in Council's Strategic and Operational Plans, and its 2014 Greenhouse Action Plan, Council programs will continue to initiate and promote actions to reduce its own greenhouse gas emissions, and implement climate change mitigation and adaptation measures. THAT Council staff prepare a report on updated targets for reduction in consumption of electricity, natural gas, water, vehicle fuel, paper and waste in Council operations, with details of current and possible Council programs in those areas generating greenhouse gas emissions. THAT Council staff provide a briefing on possible programs related to emissions reductions or other climate-related areas targeted at the community in the Canada Bay Local Government Area. THAT Council calls on state and federal governments to contribute additional funding to support local government programs dealing with climate change, and to accelerate action at state and federal levels to reduce all types of emissions. The declaration precedes the City of Canada Bay's draft Environmental Strategy and Emissions Reduction Action Plan which will be on exhibition toward the end of the year. RPJMD Kota Manado - menekankan arah pembangunan berkelanjutan dengan prioritas penataan ruang ramah lingkungan, pengendalian kawasan kumuh, penanggulangan banjir, serta rehabilitasi pesisir dan mangrove. KLHS (Kajian Lingkungan Hidup Strategis) - digunakan untuk menilai dampak kebijakan pembangunan jangka menengah terhadap daya dukung lingkungan, termasuk risiko banjir, longsor, dan abrasi. Hasil KLHS kemudian menjadi masukan dalam penyusunan RPJMD agar kebijakan lebih adaptif terhadap perubahan iklim.

RTRW Kota Manado - mengatur pemanfaatan ruang dengan mempertimbangkan daya dukung lingkungan, perlindungan kawasan lindung (semisal hutan dan mangrove), serta pengendalian alih fungsi lahan yang menjadi salah satu penyebab utama banjir dan degradasi lingkungan.

Rencana Pengelolaan Lingkungan Hidup Daerah (RPLHD) - menjadi dokumen dasar pengelolaan kualitas lingkungan, termasuk pengendalian pencemaran udara, pengelolaan sampah, dan rehabilitasi ekosistem pesisir.

Rencana Aksi Daerah Adaptasi Perubahan Iklim (RAD-API) - meskipun belum berdiri sendiri, beberapa elemen adaptasi sudah terintegrasi dalam kebijakan sektor, misalnya program drainase kota, early warning system banjir, serta penyediaan ruang terbuka hijau untuk ketahanan iklim.

Dengan kombinasi dokumen ini, terlihat bahwa Kota Manado berusaha mengarusutamakan isu lingkungan dan iklim ke dalam pembangunan jangka menengah dan tata ruang, meskipun tantangan masih ada pada aspek pendanaan, koordinasi lintas sektor, dan implementasi teknis.

col8_Comment: The Boulder County Coordinated Plan, also known as Mobility and Access for All Ages and Abilities, builds off the Boulder County Transportation Master Plan and serves as a new guide for Boulder County's multimodal transportation policy as it pertains to populations with special needs. People from dozens of local organizations—human services, school districts, transportation providers, community-based organizations, and government at the municipal, county, regional, and state levels—contributed to this planning process by sharing perspectives, feedback, and aspirations. The Boulder County Comprehensive Plan (BCCP) reflects Boulder County's tradition of serving as a leader in environmental and land stewardship, along with the county's commitment to sustainability, climate resilience and equity. The BCCP was developed to respond to the widely accepted principle that the county will make decisions affecting the future of the county's lands in a coordinated and responsible manner. Since its initial adoption in 1978, the overall philosophy of the Plan has changed very little; the county's vision is to channel growth to municipalities, to protect agricultural lands, and to prioritize preservation of our environmental and natural resources in making land use and related decisions. The Plan's Guiding Principles, adopted in 2012, expand upon this longstanding vision to recognize the critical importance of factoring social equity into decision making, and weighing the interconnections among social, environmental and economic factors in all decisions.The Plan is intended to serve as a policy reference for all decisions affecting land use and community planning in Boulder County. This includes operational and program planning decisions by leadership across all county departments, open space acquisition, transportation planning, long range land use planning, housing, and other topics. The Plan is most commonly referenced in the development review process because the Boulder County Land Use Code requires that land use decisions are consistent with the Plan. However, the intent is for the Plan's goals and policies to serve as a guide for strategic and master planning efforts county-wide.

Future conditions for this project, which can be impacted by development and redevelopment, climate change, and sea level rise (SLR), are the 2040, 2070, and 2100 planning horizons. Additionally, flood impacts were analyzed for 2100 using National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Intermediate-High SLR scenario. Results were used to evaluate sensitivity to current and potential flooding impacts and identify areas of concern. Strategy and action plans were provided to ensure that the flood hazards of 3-, 10-, and 25-year storm events are not increased by future development.\nCity staff collaboratively developed a suite of watershed management measures that are diverse in scope. These measures can be applied equitably across the City and are supported by the scientific findings of this WMP and previous City studies. This diverse menu of strategies ensures that the City is more resilient to potential future changes in the watershed. When combined, implemented, and monitored correctly, these strategies will likely provide appreciable and synergistic flood relief in future conditions for storm events up to and including the 25-year storm event. Because this study also included information up to the 100-year storm event for both current and future conditions, the City can expect some relief in larger storm events by applying these measures. However, given the size of those events and the hydrography of South Florida, the City cannot completely mitigate larger storm events and the City's success in flood mitigation will vary in future years.

col8_Comment:
O Município da Figueira da Foz elaborou o seu Plano de Ação do Plano Estratégico de Resíduos Sólidos Urbanos (PAPERSU), em articulação com a publicação do Plano Estratégico para os Resíduos Urbanos (PERSU 2030), aprovado pela Resolução do Conselho de Ministros n.º 30/2023, de 24 de março, que determinou que os Sistemas Municipais de Gestão de Resíduos devem apresentar os PAPERSU 2030, que traduzam as estratégias definidas e as medidas a adotar para o cumprimento das ambiciosas metas ambientais até 2035.

Sendo as metas de reciclagem estabelecidas extremamente desafiantes, os resultados dependerão da contribuição individual de cada um neste processo, tendo presente que até 2030, 60% dos resíduos urbanos produzidos terão de ser reciclados e em 2035 apenas 10% dos resíduos poderão ser depositados em aterro.
Neste âmbito, a Câmara Municipal está a definir um conjunto de projetos e iniciativas que visam a prevenção e reutilização de resíduos e o alcance das metas de reciclagem para 2030 em 22% na recolha seletiva das 3 frações (papel, plástico e vidro) e em 28% no tratamento de resíduos orgânicos/biorresíduos (seja através da recolha seletiva ou compostagem.
O Plano encontra--se para validação final da entidade responsável (Agência Portuguesa do Ambiente).

col8_Comment: A Agenda de Sustentabilidade - Floresta, Biodiversidade e Desenvolvimento Rural do Concelho de Loulé 2020-2025 encontra-se enquadrada na Estratégia Municipal de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas (EMAAC), no Plano Municipal de Ação Climática (PMAC) e no Plano Municipal de Defesa da Floresta Contra Incêndios (PMDFCI) de Loulé, concorrendo também para os objetivos do aspirante Geoparque Algarvensis (rede de Geoparques Mundiais da UNESCO), projeto conjunto dos Municípios de Loulé, Silves e Albufeira.Na perspetiva de um novo olhar sobre a floresta mediterrânica de uso múltiplo e o pomar tradicional de sequeiro, sistemas agrários em degradação e desvalorização, com o abandono de vastas áreas do barrocal e da serra, mas também, no sentido de conhecer o potencial do capital natural do concelho, avançou a avaliação, mapeamento e valoração dos serviços dos ecossistemas. O município encontra-se assim atualmente dotado de um mapeamento de habitats e espécies RELAPE (Raras, Endémicas, Localizadas, Ameaçadas ou em Perigo de Extinção) de fauna e flora com potencial de ocorrência no território, sendo que para cada uso do solo foi realizada uma avaliação qualitativa do potencial de fornecimento de serviços dos ecossistemas de aprovisionamento, regulação e culturais.A definição de uma estratégia ampla para o interior, passa pela concretização de projetos estruturantes que permitam dar uma projeção temporal, mobilizar os atores do território para novos modelos de intervenção, valorizar a ação dos “cuidadores do território”, ativar programas de preservação genética e melhoramento de plantas de espécies mediterrânicas, promover a geração de inovação para novos negócios a partir da bioeconomia circular.

col5_Boundary of plan relative to jurisd: Same - covers entire jurisdiction and nothing else
col8_Comment: O aumento da procura de água, os padrões de consumo e os impactes das alterações climáticas, nomeadamente do aumento das temperaturas e da variabilidade nos padrões de precipitação, constituem grandes desafios para a gestão dos recursos hídricos, um recurso escasso e estratégico. A sua gestão é particularmente desafiante em regiões onde a procura pelos recursos hídricos é elevada e a oferta depende da sazonalidade, da interanualidade e das diferenças espaciais de precipitação. Todos estes desafios caracterizam a região do mediterrâneo, onde se insere Portugal continental, sendo particularmente notório na região do Algarve, e consequentemente no concelho de Loulé.Consciente dos desafios que o seu território enfrenta, o município de Loulé reconhece o seu posicionamento e a posição proactiva que necessita adotar para implementar soluções promotoras de uma gestão eficiente e sustentável do recurso Água, razão pela qual integrou, em março de 2021, a Rede “CAPT2 - Circularidade da Água: Por todos e Para Todos”, uma candidatura conjunta com outros municípios portugueses, ao eixo temático “Ciclo Urbano da Água” da Iniciativa Cidades Circulares, promovida pela Direção Geral do Território. A rede CAPT2, parceria liderada pelo Laboratório da Paisagem (Guimarães), e que envolveu os municípios de Águeda, Lagoa (Açores), Loulé, Mértola, Oeiras, Oliveira de Frades e Ponte de Sor, teve como objeto focal o desenvolvimento de um Plano Local de Ação Integrada (PLAI) para promover a circularidade da água em cada um dos territórios envolvidos, assente num modelo de governança que integrou as componentes técnicas e participativas, e no qual foi imprescindível o envolvimento efetivo dos atores locais. o PLAI de Loulé constitui um instrumento de cariz operacional, articulado com os demais referenciais estratégicos locais e regionais, e que assenta na implementação de 6 ações principais, num horizonte temporal de 5 anos. O PLAI de Loulé prossegue, entre outros, a valorização dos recursos hídricos, a dinamização de iniciativas promotoras da eficiência hídrica e da circularidade da água em meio urbano, o desenvolvimento de projetos e medidas relacionadas com o aproveitamento de águas pluviais e reutilização de águas residuais tratadas, bem como de água proveniente de origens alternativas à rede de abastecimento, numa lógica de proximidade, e o desenvolvimento de um modelo de governança local participativo, aumentando a capacidade adaptativa e de resiliência da população.

col8_Comment: Cornwall's Local Flood Risk Management Strategy 2020 sets out how Cornwall Council and its partner authorities intend to work together to manage flood risk from all sources. Will be reviewed in 2026. •We will work with our communities and other Flood Risk Management organisations to manage the likelihood and impact of flooding and coastal change for the benefit of our communities, visitors, businesses and environment • We will support local people and businesses to take part in managing the risks that affect them. • We will coordinate information sharing, plan making, prioritising investment and effective project implementation • We will prioritise high risk locations for proposed improvement schemes. This vision for managing flood risks in Cornwall is underpinned by seven overarching and crosscutting themes: A Working together B Communities C Development planning and regeneration D Working with natural processes E Prioritising and funding F Resilient Cornwall G Multiple benefits Each theme is supported by a high-level vision, activities and achievements since the first Strategy which is explained in Section 3. Cornwall's Local Flood Risk Management Strategy covers 2020 to 2026 and comprises 3 parts: •Part 1: Strategic Vision outlines the responsibilities of the Risk Management Authorities in Cornwall. It details how they are working in partnership to coordinate local flood risk management. Following review, it includes an increased emphasis on climate change impacts and the need for adaptation. It also included Nature-Based Solutions and Property Flood Resilience. •Part 2: Local Flood Risk Management Profiles will provide information on high priority communities and will be continually developed and updated. They provide specific information relevant to flood risk management for each town or community and bring together information from multiple sources. They provide a compilation of flood risk data for ease of reference and set out known issues and evidence to identify actions that can help manage flooding at a local level. They are supported by Cornwall Council's strategic flood risk mapping facility. More communities are included as and when possible. •Part 3: Local Flood Risk Management Action Plan will be issued annually. Cornwall Council has adopted this Local Flood Risk Management Strategy to guide the development of policy and programmes across its operations and in its work with other organisations, communities and stakeholders.

col8_Comment: Decision Making Wheel (CDDW): Ensuring all key decisions take into account social, economic and environmental impacts and can ensure that people aren't negatively impacted. The wheel is being used for Cabinet decisions and within service plans, placing people and the climate at the heart of everything we do. The tool is divided into thematic segments with each segment focusing on different key areas of potential impact. Land Use: How we use the land available to us has many potential impacts on things such as wildlife, housing and the scenic quality of the landscape. Soil and Waterway Health: Any activity which would affect the concentration of carbon, nitrogen or phosphorus in the natural environment Biodiversity: Amount or type of biodiversity present in the natural environment Greenhouse Gas Emissions: Any direct or indirect impacts of the project or initiative that may increase or decrease greenhouse gas emissions being released into the atmosphere. Renewable Energy: increases or decreases the provision of renewable energy directly, or affects the likelihood of renewable energy being used or created in the future. Ocean Health: Any project or initiative that will mean a change to the chemical makeup, or wildlife contained within the ocean, locally or indirectly further afield. Water Resources: Any decision involving the increased or decreased use of water and / or pressures on the existing sewerage systems, e.g housing development. Chemical and Plastic Pollution: Consider potential additional or reduction in pollution from the environment. Air Quality: Air pollution happens when harmful or excessive quantities of substances are present in the air. Cornwall Council is committed to ensuring that we deliver procurement in a responsible way. The Responsible Procurement policy was updated in April 2021 and sets out our principles to ensure that the council follows the general principles to deliver value for money, meet the needs of residents and achieve additional economic, social and environmental benefits. The Council incorporates value for money of the goods, services and works it procures, reducing our carbon emissions, ethical sourcing and compliance with legislation within our responsible procurement policy. 
We are also drafting a Supply Chain Decarbonisation Strategy at the moment, set to be introduced in 2025. It is designed to specifically target emissions associated with the goods, works and services the Council purchases and will promote positive impacts wherever practical, and look at whole life costs of delivery. A large proportion of Cornwall's total emissions are outside of our direct control but within our influence, and this includes emissions from our supply chain. Our aim is to facilitate local leadership to influence the action of our partners and suppliers through leveraging the Council's purchasing power to get suppliers to reduce carbon emissions as a competitive part of the tendering process. This will foster a more self-reliant, sustainable and diverse local supply chain. All procurements in scope will require a relevant focus on reducing carbon emissions, which will be monitored inc. vehicle emissions, energy use, embodied carbon within materials and products and planning for a changing environment. The principles of the new Strategy have already been trialled in several procurement and commissioning exercises including with our Homecare provision contract, emissions reductions there focusing on reducing carbon-intensive travel. 
In addition, in order to support the Council's own service design process category guidance was produced to help to embed targeted carbon objectives within our sourcing process. The documents covered 8 sourcing categories and subcategories and detail specific interventions for each.

col8_Comment: Our work priorities associated with the Biodiversity Action Plan include:•Establish partnership with Natural England, LA's and North of Tyne Combined Authority to begin work on the Local Nature Recovery Strategy•Review of Biodiversity Action Plan (BAP) targets.•Commence work on Biodiversity Net Gains Strategy to support the implementation of the statutory requirement of developments to deliver a 10% biodiversity net gain by 2023.•Explore opportunities to create a Biodiversity Net Gain working group with local partners to identify delivery areas.•Designate areas of the River Tyne Riverside as a Local Wildlife Site due to the presence of priority butterfly species including Dingy Skipper, Grayling and Wall.Biodiversity net gain' (or BNG) is a term used to describe an approach to development that leaves the natural environment in a measurably better state than it was beforehand. Net gains are calculated in units which can be achieved onsite (within a development boundary) through habitat creation / enhancement via landscaping or green infrastructure and / or offsite (outside a development boundary) through habitat creation / enhancement on land holdings or via habitat banks / biodiversity credits. Currently, although certain sites are protected, there are limited mechanisms to value, maintain, enhance or create wider habitats. As a result, habitats continue to be lost to development, reducing nature's ability to connect and thrive. In the future, most developments will need to deliver a minimum 10% BNG calculated using a Biodiversity Metric (which takes into account habitat size, habitat condition, habitat distinctiveness and strategic significant of the habitat) and receive approval of a net gain plan. The habitat must be secured for at least 30 years via obligations or conservation covenants. A national register of net gain delivery sites is to be established and maintained. Biodiversity net gain does not apply to Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects (NSIPs) or marine development.

col8_Comment: The WMCA defines inclusive growth as: A more deliberate and socially purposeful model of growth, measured not only by how fast or aggressive it is; but also, by how well it is created and shared across the whole population and place, and by the social and environmental outcomes it realises for our people. The Inclusive Growth Framework translates inclusive growth from an intellectual concept to into a reality that can be put into practice to build a fairer, greener and better connected region. Traditional metrics of economic vitality such as growth, jobs, and trade do not tell us enough. They don't tell who is involved in creating growth, who is (and isn't) benefiting from that growth, or which social and environmental outcomes (good and bad) result from that growth. Existing economic models are not fit-for-purpose: it externalises the inconvenient and creates an unhelpful divide between public investments and private ones. The Inclusive Growth Framework intends to change that. It focuses all types of investment - public, private, capital, revenue, time, attention - on the same set of social and environmental missions. These missions - the eight 'fundamentals' of inclusive growth - also connect to one another, ensuring that the real people, places, and businesses across the WMCA are not lost in thematic silos. The fundamentals are derived by grouping the Sustainable Development Goals in a way which is relates to the WMCA area and are structured using Kate Raworth's 'Doughnut Economics' model. The Inclusive Growth Framework is embedded into all that we do in the West Midlands Combined Authority. It was approved by the WMCA Board in September 2018 and forms the basis of our West Midlands Outcomes Framework.\nTo support the embedding of Inclusive Growth across the organisation, the WMCA has developed an Inclusive Growth Implementation Toolkit (ITK). The ITK is a self-service survey-based toolkit for members of staff which provides tailored feedback on how well projects align with the eight fundamentals of Inclusive Growth. The ITK also provides recommendations for how to boost the alignment of the project. The ITK has been developed to be used at the design, decision making and evaluation stage of the development of all projects.\nMore information available here: https://www.wmca.org.uk/what-we-do/inclusive-growth/.

As an update to the 2018 Regional Energy Strategy, in 2025 the WMCA published a new Regional Energy Strategy (RES). The new strategy recognises the changing energy landscape since 2018, including the existence of the National Energy Systems Operator (NESO); the strategy will ensure that Regional Energy Strategic Planning takes a place-based, whole system approach to planning for energy infrastructure with NESO. The new RES also recognises the advance of the WMCA; the WMCA has secured a Trailblazer Devolution Deal with the Government to pilot a single integrated settlement including retrofit funding, with new powers on energy and net zero confirmed in the 2025 Devolution White Paper. The new RES has five strategic priorities:
1)	Smart Spatial Planning- Ensuring that energy system planning is joined up with transport and spatial planning to enable the region to achieve its clean growth objectives.
2)	Local flexibility- A smarter energy system requires technologies that enable energy generation and demand to be balanced more effectively. This strategy will set out how the benefits of flexibility can be retained locally to support the decarbonisation of our built environment and transport systems.
3)	Co-located clean generation- Ensuring that renewable energy generation can increase within the West Midlands, by locating it close to demand, to avoid putting pressure on the electricity network.
4)	Skilled workforce and supply chain- Ensuring that the West Midlands is recognised as a hub of energy systems expertise, playing its part to make the entire UK energy system smarter, and growing sustainable demand for local supply chains to develop, integrated with skills and training offers.
5)	Commercial and financial innovation- Directing the region's innovation efforts towards creating business models and finance products that help to overcome barriers and accelerate the delivery of smart energy systems.

Having received political sign-off in November 2023, the WMCA produced a regional Air Quality Framework, outlining the actions that need to be taken to radically improve public health, and environmental, outcomes for people and places across the region. With support of key regional stakeholders, a high-level options paper has been produced, indicating a potential 146 interventions that could be taken at a local, regional and national level to improve air quality in the West Midlands. There is a public draft of this available: https://governance.wmca.org.uk/documents/s11066/DRAFT%20WM%20AQ%20Framework.pdf 
Following a consultation event in August 2023, the WMCA was able to finalise and publish a framework implementation plan: https://www.wmca.org.uk/media/lkchqkr4/wmca-air-framework-implementation-plan-2024-2026.pdf 
The WMCA has established an Air Quality Framework Delivery group, which is using funding provided by the WMCA board to deliver key priorities for the framework, including work on planning guidance, schools engagement and stretch targets. Alongside the delivery of the Air Quality Framework the WMCA has been successful in securing £1 million from Defra to further the air quality work. 
Using this funding, in January 2025 the WMCA launched a region-wide sensor network, with 90 sensors monitoring PM2.5. The network is aiding in providing greater 
spatial resolution on air pollutant concentrations, helping WMCA and local authorities to gain a greater understanding of air quality within the region, at the same time providing the public with easily accessible information on concentrations through a public-facing data platform. The WMCA has also ran 7 behaviour change campaigns on air quality, with a range of trials put in place to test what worked, and which best suited the regional needs, before we look to scale these up. The WMCA also ran a small grant funded programme for the local community to improve air quality and awareness and developed an air quality literacy programme. 
To continue to progress the framework, in 2025/26, the WMCA will be launching an air quality alert system, to help people within the West Midlands better understand daily air quality concentrations and provide advice on how to reduce personal exposure and reduce emissions during heightened air pollutant events. Planning guidance will also be produced to ensure air quality is considered within the planning process and an air quality schools toolkit.

col8_Comment: In July 2025 the WMCA launched the West Midlands Growth Plan, outlining a 10 year strategy for growing the region's economy. The plan outlined the intention to drive net zero innovation, including in energy systems, with the West Midlands holding a nationally recognised competitive edge in energy systems, underpinned by a strong industrial base and a dynamic innovation ecosystem. The plan establishes the ambition for the region to become the strategic centre for smart energy systems, commercializing new technologies such as smart home systems, smart business energy systems and smart heat systems. col8_Comment:
The Environmental Policy is the starting point for the municipality's work on ecological sustainability. The policy reflects the political ambitions of Laholm Municipality in the field of environment. It applies to the municipality's committees and municipally owned companies.

The foundations for Laholm's sustainability work are the municipality's vision, the UN's global Sustainable Development Goals (Agenda 2030), the Swedish National Environmental Objectives, and the sustainability principles of Sweden's Eco-municipalities.

The overarching goal of environmental policy is to hand over to the next generation a society in which the major environmental problems have been solved, without causing increased environmental and health problems beyond Sweden's borders. (According to the Swedish Parliament's definition of the Generational Goal)

Laholm Municipality shall work to:

achieve sustainable community development and reduce the municipality's overall environmental impact

translate national and global goals into practical action in operations, for example through urban planning, construction, procurement, and education

set environmental requirements in procurement and purchasing

serve as a role model in environmental work to inspire companies and others to work towards environmental goals

let resource efficiency and circular thinking permeate the municipality's operations

enable residents, businesses, and visitors to act sustainably and reduce their environmental impact

educate, inspire, and encourage employees to participate and take environmental considerations in their daily work

establish the foundation for sustainable development in preschool and school, among other things by increasing the number of environmentally certified preschools and schools

The Environmental Policy specifies important focus areas for Laholm Municipality's environmental efforts, both within the municipality's own operations and for the municipality as a whole.

col8_Comment: In September 2020, Council directed staff to develop a pilot program. With funding from the Federation of Canadian Municipalities Community Efficiency Fund, staff worked with the Centre for Climate Change Management at Mohawk College to complete the Recommendations Report for the City of Burlington's Home Retrofit Program, presented in 2022. With funding for the Better Homes Burlington Coordinator contract position approved in the 2023 budget, the Better Homes Burlington pilot program was launched in 2023. The pilot program included 20 zero-interest loans of up to $10,000 to homeowners to accelerate the adoption of air source heat pumps, as well as providing a concierge service for homeowners with guidance on options to complete a home energy efficiency retrofit. Staff launched the Better Homes Burlington concierge service in July 2023 and received applications for the zero-interest loan between September 2023 and February 2024. On May 4, 2024, Council approved the motion to continue the Better Homes Burlington Program concierge service for an additional year and approved funding to support an additional seven Better Homes Burlington program zero-interest loans. Loan applications reopened from July to December 2024. A total of 17 loans were approved through the pilot - 16 during the initial application period and 1 through the extension. Over 200 Burlington residents were assisted through the concierge service during this period. Due to low program uptake during the program extension, and the availability of alternative financial incentive programs from the Federal and Provincial Governments through the Canada Greener Homes Loan and Home Renovations Savings Program respectively, staff are not exploring funding options to continue the zero-interest loan portion of this program at this time. Staff do see merit in continuing the concierge service component of the Better Homes Burlington program. The concierge service will continue to be offered by an existing FTE position within the Emergency Management and Environmental Sustainability team. The existing FTE position will manage the concierge service by responding to residents' questions by phone and email, but will not have the capacity to promote the service as widely as was done during the pilot.

These actions to help biodiversity only need to be proportionate to the public authority's activities and functions, but every action, no matter how small, that in some way contributes to maintaining and enhancing biodiversity, will help comply with the duty. col8_Comment:
The waste plan is a steering document for waste management throughout the municipality. The waste plan 2021-2032 has a clear focus on circular economy. The municipalities are working with the waste plan's goals and there is also a collaboration network to share knowledge and take advantage of synergies between the municipalities.

Five target areas have been developed to steer towards a circular waste system:

1. Systems according to needs
To enable circular systems for materials and waste, strategic planning and a good infrastructure are required. Systems that are adapted to needs and accessible enable materials to circulate and waste to be prevented. It is important that systems for material and waste flows are planned and designed in an environmentally sustainable way so that it is easy to do the right thing now and in the future.

2. Waste is prevented
Waste quantities are reduced through a circular economy and sustainable consumption. Reuse is available to everyone and by sharing, repairing, exchanging and borrowing products, waste quantities are minimized and the amount of harmful substances in the cycle is reduced.

3. Materials circulate
Waste is material that is managed as a resource in a cycle. Through work on development and behavioral change, recycling increases to the advantage of reduced amounts of waste for incineration and landfill. Non-toxic cycles are a prerequisite for materials to circulate.

4. Food waste
Food waste is prevented while food waste is collected separately and managed as a resource. Food waste is unnecessary food waste that could have been avoided if it had been handled differently, such as stored differently or cooked and eaten. Collected food waste is managed so that plant nutrients and energy are utilized. The residues (sludge) during treatment are so clean that they can be returned to fields or forests.

5. Garbage and littering
Garbage is waste that is collected in public environments. By reducing the amount of garbage that is generated, littering is also minimized. Public environments, including water, are clean, which contributes to minimizing negative environmental impact and an increased sense of security for the public.

col4_Current status of plan: Other: Lake, Orange, Volusia, Osceola, Brevard, and Seminole County, 6 of our 8 counties, have completed individual reports. The R2C will continue the efforts with remaining counties and is incorporating Marxan conservation findings into the CCAP.

col8_Comment: Over the past several years, the Marxan spatial optimization software has been used by researchers and practitioners for spatial planning initiatives that consider watershed-based flood mitigation a core conservation objective. An ongoing research partnership between Stetson University and the East Central Florida Regional Planning Council has been employing Marxan in support of long-term flood resilience planning in counties across the region. The Marxan model simultaneously maximizes potential conservation and minimizes costs while taking available resources and a wide range of other real-world factors and constraints into consideration.\nThrough the use of the Marxan tool, Priority Natural Resources Area projects have taken place in 6 of our 8 counties across the region. Aimed to assist locally-driven conservation efforts in Lake, Orange, Osceola, Volusia, Brevard, and Seminole County, county-level conservation strategies were developed with stakeholder input and maps generated as a key result of this project, illustrating optimal environmental connectivity between currently conserved areas in the county and identified priority areas. With nearly all counties having participated in the effort, a regional picture is beginning to form with some commonalities already observed. In local stakeholder workshops, natural area layers that most often provide ecosystem services like aquifer recharge or water management are prioritized via rankings. The consideration of co-benefit factors for green space conservation, such as habitat connectivity, protection of species, and maintenance of rural economies, is also increasingly recognized as a best practice for resilience-based flood mitigation. The overall results and data gathered include the foundation to align with IUCN green standards and the development of a greater Biodiversity program applying the Singapore Index to the region while maintaining local relevance.

col8_Comment: Completed for Red Reef Park (2021) and South Beach Park (2023), these ecological restoration and management plans provide direction for restoring and maintaining coastal dune biodiversity. Every year for at least the past five years, the City has worked with City partner, the Institute for Regional Conservation (IRC), to implement the restoration and management plans. IRC works independently throughout the year to remove large tracts of invasive plants at the restoration locations and conducts eight volunteer work days annually, where invasives are removed and the dunes are replanted with native species, including endangered and threatened species. Not only does this promote biodiversity, it has the co-benefit (or primary benefit) of enhancing coastal resiliency.

col8_Comment: From the 2021 Tree Canopy Assessment, the City of Boca Raton established a goal to enhance tree canopy coverage from 26.5 to 28% by 2041. And for at least the past two years, the City has contracted with the nonprofit organization, Community Greening, on various tree canopy enhancement initiatives. Each year, Community Greening conducts three tree giveaways to residents (450 trees total, usually 3 gallon size), a drop-off of 75, 15-gallon trees to residents chosen via an application process, and a community Arbor Day planting event (40 trees, installed by volunteers under the instruction of Community Greening). With additional allocations to the City's tree canopy enhancement budget approved for FY2026, tree planting programs and initiatives will soon be expanded.\n\nAdditionally, funding was allocated for the City's Centennial Year (current) to plant a Centennial Grove of shade trees. Implementation is currently in progress. 60 trees have been planted with 40 more planned by the end of calendar year 2025.

The Local Nature Recovery Strategy considers land at a county scale and identifies locations to improve nature and provide other benefits, such as capturing carbon from the atmosphere, flood regulation and access to nature-rich spaces where this is most needed for health and wellbeing.

The Local Nature Recovery Strategy will:

Agree priorities for nature's recovery, such as increasing woodland cover or creating wetlands

Map the most valuable existing areas for nature

Map specific proposals for creating and improving habitat for nature and wider environmental goals

Decisions about where and how to recover nature will be reached through consultation with a wide range of people and groups in the area, from ecologists and community groups to health professionals and local businesses.

The LNRS helps to direct several new funding streams, including funding for farmers and land managers. It also links with Biodiversity Net Gain, which is a new planning requirement to ensure habitat for wildlife is left in a better state than it was before the development process began.

The Forest Land Use Plan (FLUP) provides a long-term framework for sustainable forest governance in Butuan City by zoning forestlands into protection and production areas, reducing open access, and ensuring tenure-based management. It envisions Butuan as a model landscape for sustainable forest management, climate-smart practices, and empowered communities that benefit from the responsible use of forest resources. By institutionalizing science-based decision-making, the plan strengthens land use governance while protecting the city's watersheds, which serve as critical water sources for both urban and rural communities.

The plan's mission emphasizes safeguarding and restoring forests through participatory governance, protecting biodiversity, and channeling resources to conservation and reforestation programs. It prioritizes the development of sub-watersheds as management units, promotes the replacement of exotic species with native trees, and identifies sustainable ecotourism opportunities. At the same time, it supports the economic viability of forest-dependent and Indigenous communities by strengthening tenure security, improving market linkages, and enhancing capacities for sustainable livelihood and enterprise development.

Aligned with the CLUP, LCCAP, DRRMP, and CDP, the FLUP ensures policy coherence and integration of forest management into broader climate action and disaster risk reduction strategies. It provides enabling mechanisms for Indigenous Peoples and CBFM communities to maximize their rights and responsibilities, access benefits from managing forestlands, and sustain tenure agreements. Through these mechanisms, the FLUP harmonizes ecological protection with social equity, ensuring that communities are both stewards and beneficiaries of forest resources.

Finally, the FLUP fosters active partnerships among local government, civil society, academe, and the private sector, supported by a multi-sectoral FLUP Technical Working Group. By promoting shared responsibility, knowledge management, and the documentation of best practices, the plan positions Butuan City as a regional model for integrated, climate-responsive forest landscape management—advancing biodiversity conservation, water security, and sustainable development for future generations.

The Transportation and Traffic Management Code of Butuan City serves as the primary regulatory framework for all transport-related duties, responsibilities, and enforcement within the city. As the foundational policy instrument, it sets the rules and standards governing vehicle operations, road use, and traffic management to ensure safe, efficient, and environmentally responsible mobility. The Code also provides the legal basis for implementing sustainable transport measures and aligns local regulations with national objectives on road safety, air quality improvement, and climate change mitigation.

A key provision of the Code is the regulation of all vehicles, focusing on efficient traffic flow, congestion reduction, and emission control. These measures not only enhance road safety but also help reduce the city's overall carbon footprint, contributing to cleaner air and a healthier environment. By integrating traffic management with sustainability principles, the Code reinforces Butuan City's commitment to building a more livable, resilient, and climate-responsive urban transport system.

In addition, the Code mandates the installation and maintenance of bike lanes and pedestrian lanes, recognizing them as essential components of active transportation infrastructure. These facilities encourage residents to walk or cycle as clean, zero-emission alternatives to motorized travel. By institutionalizing the development of such infrastructure, the Code promotes sustainable urban mobility, reduces dependence on fossil fuels, and improves public health outcomes. This integration of active transport into the regulatory framework ensures that Butuan's transportation system supports both environmental protection and inclusive, people-centered mobility.
